nātaṉāraruḷ peṟu nanti tantiṭak
kōtilā tuṇar caṉaṟ kumaraṉ kūṟiṭa
vātarāyaṇa muṉi vakuppa vōrntuṇar
cūtaṉōtiyatu mūvāṟu tolkati (kanta purāṇam)
#“makāpāratap pōrukkuppiṉ āṅkāṅku nāṭṭuk katikaḷāka vaḻaṅkiyavi ellām tiraṭṭappaṭṭaṉa. attiraṭṭu, purāṇa caṅkiti eṉṉum peyar peṟṟiruntatu. purāṇacaṅkitiyi ātāramākak koṇṭu pala purāṇaṅkaḷ eḻuntaṉa. kālantōṟum ivaṟṟuḷ piṉ cērppukaḷākap pala eḻutip pukuttappaṭṭaṉa. piramāṇṭa, vāyu, maṟca eṉpavi kālattāl muṟpaṭṭavi; pirama vivartta, civa, vāmaṉa, pākavatam eṉpavi mikap piṟkālattavi; maṟṟavi iṭikkālattavi. ivaṟṟuḷ paḻiyavi mārk kaṇṭēyamum piramamum. pirama purāṇat tiṉ pakuti paḻiyatu aṉṟāyiṉum atu āti purāṇameṉappaṭṭatu. patmapurāṇam maṟcapurāṇattukku uṟavuṭiyatākak kāṇappaṭukiṉṟatu. ataṉ perum pakuti piṟkālattatu. atil pañcatantirakkati, itōpa tēcakkati pōṉṟa nītik katikaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. purāṇaṅ kaḷāvaṉa : pirama, patma, viṭṭuṇu, civa, pākavata, nāratīya, mārkkaṇṭēya, akkiṉi, pāviciya, piramavivartta, iliṅka, varāka, iskanta, vāmaṉa, kūrma, maṟca, karuṭa, pirāmaṇṭa. ivvariciyil pukaḻpeṟṟa vāyu purāṇaṅ kāṇappaṭavilli. toṭakkattil vāyupurāṇamum piramāṇ ṭamum oṉṟāka iruntaṉa. ivviru purāṇaṅkaḷum collukkuc col ottirukkiṉṟaṉa. vāyupurāṇam kūrmapurāṇam ivviraṇṭiyum oṉṟākak koṇṭu vāyāviya piramāṇṭa eṉak kūṟukiṉṟaṉa.”
“patiṉeṭṭup purāṇaṅkaḷit tavirap patiṉeṭṭu upa purāṇaṅ kaḷumuṇṭu. ivi muṉivarkaḷāṟ ceyyappaṭṭavi eṉak kūrmapurā ṇamuṅ karuṭapurāṇamuṅ kūṟukiṉṟaṉa. avaṟṟukku mikka paḻamiyik koṭuppataṟkāka avi maṉuvāl ceyyappaṭṭavi eṉṟu patmapurā ṇam kūṟukiṉṟatu. upa purāṇaṅkaḷāvaṉa : caṉaṟkumāra, naracimma, skanta, civatarma, turvāca, mārkkaṇṭēya, kapila, vāmaṉa, ucāṉa, piramāṇṭa, varuṇa, kāḷikā, makēcuvara, cāmpa, cura, paracurāma, mārīca, pārkkava eṉpaṉa.”
taruma cāttiraṅkaḷ
29vētaṅkaḷil collappaṭum tarumaṅkaḷi allatu oḻukkaṅ kaḷit tiraṭṭik kūṟum nūlkaḷ* taruma cāttiraṅkaḷ eṉappaṭṭaṉa. ācuvalāyaṉam, pōtāyaṉam, apastampam mutaliyaṉa cūttira vaṭivil ceyyappaṭṭa paḻiya nūlkaḷ. taruma cūttiraṅkaḷit toṭarntu mikuti nūlkaḷ tōṉṟiṉa. maṉu mirutiyum yākñavalkiya mirutiyum mirutikaḷil mutaṉmiyuṭiyavi. taruma cāttiraṅkaḷ patiṉeṭṭu eṉappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. maṉu, yākñavalkiyam, nāratīyam, parācaram, pirakaspati mutaliyavum piṟavumākiya mirutikaḷ mikap paḻaṅkālattil vāḻnta iruṭikaḷiṉ peyarkaḷip peṟṟiruppiṉum avi kiṟittuvukkup pala nūṟṟāṇṭukaḷiṉ piṉ ceyyappaṭṭaṉavākak kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa.# vicayanakara aracar kālattil vittiyāraṇiyar parācara mirutikku virivuri ceytār. ammiruti nūli ātāramākak koṇṭu vicayanakara aracariṉ caṭṭaṅkaḷ ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. kiḻakkintiyak kampeṉiyār kālattil ceyyappaṭṭa intuc caṭṭam (intu lā) eṉpatu mīmāmci nūliyum miruti nūlkaḷiyum ātāramākak koṇṭu pirāmaṇarāṟ ceyyap paṭṭatu.
cūttira vaṭivil ceyyappaṭṭa taruma nūlkaḷ kutamam, pōtāyaṉam, āpastampam, vaciṭṭam, viṣṇu eṉpaṉa. miruti nūlkaḷ piṉvaruvaṉa : maṉu, attiri, viṣṇu, hāritar, *yākñavalkiyar, ucaṉar, āṅkīracar, yamar, āpastampar, camvarttar, kāttiyāyaṉar , pirakaspati, parācarar, viyācar, caṅkar, vikitar, takkar, kutamar, cātātapar, vaciṭṭar mutaliyavarkaḷiṉ peyar peṟṟavi.
vitīkattil varuṇamum varuṇāccirama tarumaṅkaḷum mukkiya muṭiyaṉa. pirāmaṇa, cattiriya, viciya, cūttira eṉṉum nāṉku varuṇaṅ kaḷum piṟappiṉāl uṇṭāṉavi. ivarkaḷukkuḷḷa nītikaḷum vev vēṟāṉavi. tamiḻnāṭṭu nīti avvāṟirukkavilli. piṟappiṉāl ellārum oru kulattiṉar; ceyyum toḻil vēṟṟumiyāl avarkaḷ vevvēṟu kulattiṉar. āyiṉum “piṟappokku mellāvuyirkkuñ ciṟappovvā - ceytoḻil vēṟṟumiyāl” (tirukkuṟaḷ) “oṉṟē kulamum oruvaṉē tēvaṉum naṉṟē niṉimiṉ” (tirumantiram) eṉkiṉ ṟaṉa tamiḻ maṟikaḷ. vaṭanāṭṭu nītikkum teṉṉāṭṭu nītikkumuḷḷa vēṟupāṭṭi, “vaḷḷuvar cey tirukkuṟaḷi vaḻuvaṟa naṉkuṇarn tōrkaḷ - uḷḷuvarō maṉuvāti oru kulattukkoru nīti” eṉṉum maṉōṉmaṇīyac ceyyuḷ iṉitu viḷakkukiṉṟatu.
teṉṉāṭṭil vitīkam
vaṭanāṭṭil āriyar tamiḻar eṉṉum iru iṉattiṉarum kalantu oṉṟupaṭṭaṉar. vitīkamum uḷnāṭṭu matamum kalappaṭintaṉa. pirāmaṇa matattiṉar, tām putitākac ceṉṟu vāḻa nērnta iṭaṅkaḷuk kēṟpa am makkaḷiṉ oḻukkaṅkaḷiyum teyvaṅkaḷiyum tammavi pōlat taḻuvik koṇṭārkaḷ. vēta matattiyum vēḷvikaḷiyum etirkkum putta matattit tōṟṟuvitta kutama puttariyē avarkaḷ viṭṭuṇuviṉ avatāramākkit tamatu kaṭavuḷaruḷ cērttuk koṇṭārkaḷ.#
pattirapāku eṉṉum camaṇa muṉivariṉ talimiyil muriya cantirakuptaṉum pala camaṇa muṉivarkaḷum micūriluḷḷa pelakoḷa eṉṉumiṭattukkuc ceṉṟu taṅkiṉārkaḷeṉat teṉṉintiya camaṇar kaḷiṉ varalāṟu kūṟukiṉṟatu. ivarkaḷi aṭuttup pirāmaṇarkaḷum puttarum teṟkē vantirukkalām.31 pirāmaṇar tamatu matattip parappum nōkkamākavō, atikāratti nāṭṭavirumpiyō iṅku varavilli. tolkāppiyam ceyyappaṭukiṉṟa kālattil ivarkaḷ tamiḻnāṭṭil iruntārkaḷ. vaṭanāṭṭup pirāmaṇar vaḻakkukaḷ cilavaṟṟōṭu tamiḻ vaḻakkukaḷ oppiṭṭuk kūṟappaṭṭirukkiṉṟaṉa. caṅka kālattil aṅkumiṅkum cila vitīka matattiṉar vāḻntu koṇṭirun tārkaḷ. avarkaḷ tamiḻar camayak koḷkikaḷil māṟṟattic ceyyakkūṭiya avvaḷavu peruntokiyiṉarāka irukkavilli.32
yākaṅkaḷ ceyvatāl pakivarip pōril vellalām, celvam atikarikkum, āyuḷ perukum eṉṉum nampikkikaḷ iruntaṉa. tamiḻ aracaruṭ cilar in nampikkikaḷil tōyntu pirāmaṇap purōkitar vāyilāka yākaṅkaḷ ceytaṉar.33 itu caṅka kāla aracarkaḷ cilarukku “irācacūyam vēṭṭaṭa”, “palyāka cāli” mutaliya aṭi moḻikaḷ vaḻaṅkiyami koṇṭu aṟiya varukiṉṟatu.
āṅkilattil varalāṟu eḻutiyavarkaḷ tamiḻil antaṇar eṉṉum coṟ kāṇappaṭṭāl ati pirāmaṇar eṉṟu moḻipeyarttiruk kiṟārkaḷ. maṟṟiya nāṭukaḷil pōlavē tamiḻ nāṭṭil camaya karumaṅkaḷik kaṇkāṇikkum kurumār iruntārkaḷ. ivarkaḷ antaṇar eṉavum, pārppaṉareṉavum, purōkitar eṉavum aṟiyappaṭṭārkaḷ. ippeyarkaḷi ellām pirāmaṇaṉ eṉṟu moḻipeyarttatiṉāl tamiḻ nāṭṭil camayamirukkavilli, kurumārirukkavilli, kurumār vaṭanāṭṭiṉiṉṟum vantaṉar; camayamum vaṭanāṭṭiṉiṉṟu vantatu eṉṟum tavaṟāṉa koḷkikaḷ eḻukiṉṟaṉa.
vaṭa nāṭṭār paṭiyeṭuppu 
muṟkālattil tamiḻ nāṭṭukku vaṭakkē taṇṭakam eṉṉum peruṅkāṭu iruntatu. atu ippōtiya orissā, āntirap piratēcam, mattiyap piratēcam eṉpavaṟṟi aṭakkiya parappāka iruntatu. tamiḻ nāṭṭil vāḻntu koṇṭirunta makkaḷē vaṭakku nōkkic ceṉṟu vintiya malittoṭar variyil kuṭiyēṟiṉārkaḷ. vintiyattukkut teṟkil vāḻnta ellā makkaḷum toṭakkattil orē moḻiyum paṇpāṭum uṭiyavarkaḷāka iruntārkaḷ. vitīka matam vaṭanāṭṭi ṉiṉṟum teṟku nōkki vantu koṇṭiruntatu. vitīkariṉ moḻi camakkirutamāka iruntatu. putta camaṇa mataṅkaḷum teṟku nōkki vantaṉa. immataṅkaḷiṉ moḻikaḷ, pirākirutaṅkaḷum camakkirutamumāka iruntaṉa. pirākirutaṅkaḷum camakkirutamum teṟkē vāḻnta makkaḷiṉ moḻiyōṭu kalantaṉa. ataṉāl kaṉṉaṭam, teluṅku, tuḷu, mali yāḷam mutaliya moḻikaḷ tōṉṟiṉa.
kaliṅkam āntiram mutaliya nāṭukaḷ nantar muriyar mutaliya vaṭa nāṭṭār āḷukikkuṭpaṭṭiruntaṉa. muriya āṭci vīḻntapiṉ cātavākaṉar eṉṉum aracar āntira nāṭṭi āṇṭaṉar. muriyar āṭciyil atikārikaḷāka iruntavarkaḷ avvāṭci oḻintapiṉ kaṭṭuppāṭaṟṟa ciṟṟaracarkaḷāyiṉar. ivarkaḷ pirāmaṇarākavum vitīka matattilum camakkirutattilum paṟṟuṭiyavarkaḷākavumiruntārkaḷ. acuvamētam mutaliya vēḷvikaḷic ceytu vantārkaḷ.34 tamiḻ nāṭṭiṉiṉṟum ceṉṟu vaṭakkē kuṭiyēṟiya āriyamayamāṉavarkaḷē āntirar eṉa varalāṟṟāciriyarkaḷ kūṟiyirukkiṉṟārkaḷ. ciṟī cātakarṇi eṉṉum cātavākaṉa aracaṉ (ki.mu.189) periya yākaṅkaḷic ceytā ṉeṉṟum yākattiṟ purōkitarāka irunta pirāmaṇarukkup pattāyirak kaṇakkāṉa pacukkaḷiyum , āyirakkaṇakkāṉa kutirikaḷiyum, anēkam yāṉikaḷiyum pala kirāmaṅkaḷiyum, pattāyirakkaṇakkāṉa kārcap paṇattiyum tāṉamākak koṭuttāṉeṉṟum oru cācaṉam kūṟukiṉṟatu. ivvāṟu āntira nāṭu vitīkamayamāka iruntatu.
cātavākaṉar vīḻcci aṭinta pōtu avarkaḷiṉ kīḻ atikāri kaḷāka iruntōr kaṭṭuppāṭaṟṟa ciṟṟaracarkaḷāka māṟiṉar. ivarkaḷil cilar ki.pi. āṟām nūṟṟāṇṭil tamiḻnāṭṭiṉmītu paṭi eṭut tārkaḷ. ivarkaḷ cōḻa nāṭṭiṉ oru pakutiyākiya toṇṭi nāṭṭiveṉṟu kāñcīpurattit talinakarākak koṇṭu pattām nūṟṟāṇṭuvari āṭci purintārkaḷ. ivarkaḷ pallavar eṉa aṟiyap paṭṭārkaḷ. ivarkaḷ tamiḻaṟiyātavar; vitīka matattiṉar; camakkirutak kalvikkup pērātaravu aḷittavar.35 pallavarkālac cācaṉamoṉṟu iskantavarmaṉ pārattuvāca kōttirattavaṉ eṉak kūṟukiṉṟatu. pallavarit toṭarntu vaṭakkil niṉṟum teṟkē paṭi eṭuttu vantavarkaḷ irāṭṭira kūṭar, katampar, kaṅkar, hōycalar, cāḷukkiyar, kākatīyar eṉap palarāvar. ivarkaḷil puttam allatu camaṇattit taḻuvāta aracar vitīkarākavum vaṭamoḻip paṟṟuṭiyarāy ataṉi ātarippōrākavum iruntaṉar. kaṭampa aracar pirāmaṇa vamicattavarāka iruntaṉar.36 mayūravarmaṉ eṉṉum katampa aracaṉ (ki.pi.345-360) patiṉeṭṭu acuvamētayākaṅkaḷ purintu pala kirāmaṅkaḷip pirāmaṇa rukkut tāṉam vaḻaṅkiyatip paṟṟic cācaṉam oṉṟu kūṟukiṟatu.
vicayanakara aracāṅkam vitīkamayamāka iruntatu. vittiyaraṇiyar parācaramirutikku uri eḻutiṉār. avar uriyiyum, mirutiyiyum taḻuvi aracāṅkac caṭṭaṅkaḷ ceyyappaṭṭaṉa. camakkirutak kalviyi vaḷarp pataṟku perumuyaṟci ceyyappaṭṭatu.* piṟkālattil āriyak koḷki kaḷit taḻuviya teṉṉāṭṭaracar tammic cattiriyar eṉak kūṟik koṇṭu pūṇūl tarittaṉar# paṇṭit tamiḻaracar ivvāṟu ceytu koḷḷavilli.
kōyilkaḷ
vitīkariṉ vaḻipāṭu yāka muṟiyākavum, teṉṉāṭṭiṉar vaḻipāṭu kōyil muṟiyākavum iruntaṉa. vētaṅkaḷil kōyilamit tal, kōyil kiriyikaḷ ceytal, tiruvinteḻuttu ōtutal, tirunīṟu pūcutal pōṉṟavaṟṟukku vitikaḷum viḷakkaṅkaḷum kiṭiyā. kōyil vaḻipāṭu, viḻākkaḷ avaṟṟiṉ viḷakkaṅkaḷ pōlvaṉa ākamaṅkaḷil kūṟappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. kōyil kiriyikaḷ cila karuttukkaḷi viḷakkum apinayaṅkaḷ eṉa aṟiñar kūṟukiṉṟaṉar. itu kāraṇamākavē tēvatāci vaḻakkam kōyilkaḷil iruntu vantatu. muṟkālattil kallāleṭuk kappaṭṭa kōyilkaḷ nakaraṅkaḷilēyē iruntaṉa. ēṉiya iṭaṅkaḷil niḻal maraṅkaḷiṉ kīḻ civaliṅkaṅkaḷ vittu vaḻipaṭappaṭṭaṉa. piṟ kālattil avvaruṭ kuṟikaḷic cuṟṟik kaṭṭaṭamamikkappaṭṭatu. kuttā lattil ālum palāvum, tirunelvēliyil mūṅkilum, maturiyil kaṭampum, tiruvāṉikkāvil nāvalum, citamparattil tilliyum, tiruvoṟṟiyūril makiḻamum talamaraṅkaḷāka iruttal itaṟkuc cāṉ ṟākum. ellā makkaḷum uyarvu tāḻvu eṉṉum vēṟupāṭiṉṟi aruḷ taṟikaḷi vaḻipaṭṭārkaḷ. aruṭkuṟiyiyum ataṉic cūḻnta iṭat tiyum mēṟpārttuk kaṭavuḷi arccittavarkaḷ pārppār eṉap paṭṭaṉar. pārppār eṉpataṟku mēṟpārppavar eṉpatu poruḷ.
vaṭanāṭṭiṉiṉṟum vanta pallavar hōycaḷar, kaṅkar, cāḷuk kiyar, irāṭṭira kūṭar mutaliya aracar vitīka camayattavarkaḷāka irun tārkaḷ; civaṉ tirumāl mutaliya kaṭavuḷariyum vaḻipaṭṭārkaḷ. kōyil kaḷil vēḷāṇ marapic cērnta tēcikar pōṉṟavarkaḷ arccakarāka iruntu vantārkaḷ. avarkaḷ tamiḻil tutipāṭik kaṭavuḷip pūcit tārkaḷ. kōyil vaḻipāṭukaḷik kūṟum ākamaṅkaḷ tamiḻilēyē iruntaṉa.
“muttiyi ñāṉatti muttamiḻ ōciyi”
“tamiḻmaṇ ṭalamintun tāviya ñāṉa
mumiḻvatu pōla vulakan tirivar
aviḻu maṉamumem māti yaṟivum
tamiḻmaṇ ṭalamintun tattuvamāmē”
“catācivan tattuva muttamiḻ vētam”
“centami ḻāti teḷintu vaḻipaṭu
nantiyitaṉi navamurittāṉē”
“īṟāṉa kaṉṉi kumariyē kāviri
vēṟā navatīrtta mikkuḷḷa veṟpēḻuḷ
pēṟāṉa vētākamamē piṟatta lāṉ
māṟāta teṉṟici viyakañ cuttamē”
eṉavarum tirumantirac ceyyuṭkaḷ civacittānta ñāṉamum ākamaṅ kaḷum tamiḻiliruntaṉa eṉpatit terivikkiṉṟaṉa. vitīka camayatti mēlākak koṇṭa aracar pārppāri vilakkip pirāmaṇari arccaka rāka amarttiṉar. avarkaḷ tamiḻaṟiyātavarum kōyil kiriyikaḷi aṟiyātavarumāka iruntārkaḷ. ākavē kōyil vaḻipāṭṭukku viḷakkam kūṟum ākamaṅkaḷ vaṭamoḻippaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa.* ippoḻutu vaṭa moḻiyil kāṇappaṭum ākamaṅkaḷ eḻutappaṭṭuḷḷa camakkiruta naṭi ki.pi. 10ām nūṟṟāṇṭic cērntateṉa ārāycci aṟiñar kūṟukiṉ ṟaṉar. vaṭa moḻippaṭuttappaṭṭa ākamaṅkaḷiṉiṭiyiṭiyē vitīkak karuttukkaḷum pukuttappaṭṭaṉa. vaṭamoḻippaṭuttappaṭṭapiṉ tamiḻ nūlkaḷ aḻikkappaṭṭaṉa. tilliyil tēvāraṅkaḷ pūṭṭivikkappaṭ ṭirunta varalāṟu ivvaki muyaṟcikaḷiloṉṟākum. puttakōcar eṉpār ciṅkaḷa moḻiyilirunta putta nūlkaḷip pāḷiyil moḻi peyarttapiṉ ciṅkaḷa nūlkaḷi ellām tiraṭṭi erittuviṭṭāreṉa varalāṟṟāciriyarkaḷ kūṟiyirukkiṉṟaṉar. itu pōṉṟa katiyē tamiḻuk kum nērntatu.#
civattukku māṟupaṭṭa vitīkar kōyil pūcakarāka amarn tatit tamiḻaṟiñar virumpavilli.
“pērkoṇṭa pārppāṉ pirāṉṟaṉṉi yarccittāl
pōrkoṇṭa vēntarkkup pollā viyātiyām
pārkoṇṭa nāṭṭukkup pañcamu māmeṉṟē
cīrkoṇṭa nanti terintu rittāṉē.”
“cattiya miṉṟit taṉiñāṉan tāṉiṉṟi
otta viṭayam viṭṭōru muṇarviṉṟi
pattiyumiṉṟip paraṉuṇmi yiṉṟiyūṇ
pittēṟu mūṭar pirāmaṇar tāmaṉṟē.”
“nūluñ cikiyum nuvaliṟ piramamō
nūlatu kāṟpāca nuṇciki kēcamā
nūlatu vētānta nuṇciki ñāṉamā
nūliṭi yantaṇar kāṇa nuvaliṉē.”
eṉṉum tirumantirac ceyyuṭkaḷ vitīkap pirāmaṇari nōkkik kūṟap paṭṭavi eṉa aṟiñar karutukiṉṟaṉar.
aruḷtaṟikaḷ allatu civaliṅkaṅkaḷic cuṟṟik kōyilkaḷ eḻuntaṉa. tamiḻ nāṭṭiṟ pirāmaṇar palar irukkavilli. ik kōyil kaḷil pūcakarāka amarttuvataṟku aracar vaṭanāṭṭiṉiṉṟum mūvāyira var nālāyiravar eṉap pirāmaṇak kuṭumpaṅkaḷik koṇṭu van tārkaḷ. avarkaḷik kōyilic cūḻavum kirāmaṅkaḷilum kuṭiyēṟ ṟiṉārkaḷ.* avarkaḷukku nilaṅkaḷum vīṭukaḷum māṉiyamāka aḷikkap paṭṭaṉa. avarkaḷukku ellā varikaḷum nīkkappaṭṭiruntaṉa.
pōtiya pirāmaṇar teṉṉāṭṭilillāmiyāl pirāmaṇa rallātārum pirāmaṇarākkappaṭṭārkaḷ. pirāmaṇa vakuppiṉar tamiḻ nāṭṭuk kurukkaḷ kuṭumpaṅkaḷilum tirumaṇañ ceytu koṇṭārkaḷ.
civa vitīka mataṅkaḷiṉ kalappu
tamiḻar camayattik kuṟittu cēṣa aiyaṅkāravarkaḷ tirāviṭa intiyā eṉṉum tamatu nūliṟ kūṟiyiruppataṉ curukkam varumāṟu: tamiḻarkaḷiṭiyē aḻakuk kalikaḷum camayamum vaḷarcciyaṭintirun taṉa. “teṉṉintiyāvil tattuvañāṉa nūlkaḷ irukkiṉṟaṉa. avaṟṟil vaṭanāṭṭuc celvākku ōraḷavu kāṇappaṭṭālum nāṭṭukkuc contamāṉa tattuvañāṉam kāṇappaṭukiṉ ṟatu. varalāṟu campantamāṉa ārāyccikku avi peritum payaṉpaṭattakkaṉa” eṉṟu māksmūlar āṟu tattuvañāṉaṅkaḷ eṉṉum nūlil kūṟiyuḷḷār. teṉṉintiya camayam taṉippaṭṭa toṭakkamuṭiyatu; piṟkālattil atu āriyac celvākkup peṟṟatu. tamiḻariṉ camayam cila vakikaḷil āriyac celvākkukku uṭpaṭavilli eṉṟum, atu āriyar camayattiṉ mītu celvākku naṭattiyateṉṟum kāṭṭa muṭiyum. vētak koḷkikaḷiyum, vētak kiriyikaḷiyum ellārum ēṟṟuk koḷḷavilli. avikaḷiṉ mutaṉmiyik kaṅki yamuṉi āṟukaḷ pāyum palam poruntiya avarkaḷ nāṭukaḷilum puttamum camaṇamum aṟikūvi etirttaṉa. uyarnta cātiyiṉar eṉappaṭṭa ciṟupāṉmiyiṉarē vētak koḷki kaḷip piṉpaṟṟiṉar; perumpālōr paḻiya uḷnāṭṭu matak koḷkikaḷip piṉpaṟṟiṉārkaḷ.
vētakālat teyvaṅkaḷiṉ peyar mūlaṅkaḷ teḷivākak kāṇap paṭavilli. appeyar mūlaṅkaḷ intu airōppiya moḻikaḷil kāṇappaṭavilli. ākavē at teyvaṅkaḷ tamiḻariṉ teyvaṅka ḷātal vēṇṭum. āriyar vaḻippaṭṭa varuṇaṉ tamiḻar teyvamātal vēṇṭum. kaṭaṟkarikaḷil vāḻnta makkaḷ vaḻipaṭṭa it teyvatti āriya iruṭikaḷ tamatu teyvaṅkaḷuḷ cērttu vaḻipaṭṭārkaḷ. āriyariṉ uruttiraṉ tamiḻar vaḻipaṭṭa iṉṉoru teyvam. uruttiraṉ eṉpatu civantavaṉ (civaṉ) eṉṉum tamiḻp peyariṉ moḻi peyarppu. veṟṟiyik koṭukkum koṟṟavi tamiḻar teyvam. āriyariṉ tuvaṭṭā eṉṉum teyvam tamiḻk kammiyariṉ teyvamākalām. tamiḻ uḻavariṉ teyvam intira vaṇakkattuḷ maṟintu viṭṭatu. civa, muruka vaṇakkaṅkaḷ āriyariṉ varukikku muṉ intiya nāṭṭil iruntaṉa. intu matattiluḷḷa civaṉ, kiruṭṭiṇaṉ, irāmar, turkki mutaliya teyvaṅkaḷum, teyvaṅkaḷiṉ avatāraṅkaḷum, maṟu piṟappuk koḷki kaḷum vētaṅkaḷ aṟiyātavi. vēta matattil kāṇappaṭum ivi allāta piṟa pōkkukaḷ pāracīkam, kirīs mutaliya nāṭukaḷil kāṇap paṭuvaṉa pōṉṟavi.
paḻantamiḻariṉ camayam civa vaḻipāṭāka iruntateṉap pōppiyar pōṉṟa aṟiñar karutiṉar. civaṉ arūpamāṉa tiyāṉa vaṭivilum, iliṅka vaṭivilum vaḻipaṭappaṭṭār eṉṟu ṭākṭar isṭipiṉcaṉ kūṟiyuḷḷār. *pūvum pukiyum koṇṭu vaḻipaṭutal paḻiya tamiḻariṉ vaḻipāṭṭu muṟi. pū itayattiyum puki aḵtu urukuvatiyum kuṟip piṭukiṉṟaṉa. irāvaṇaṉ poṉ# iliṅkattit taṉṉuṭaṉ koṇṭu ceṉṟu pūvum pukiyum koṇṭu vaḻipaṭṭāṉ. irāvaṇaṉum vāli yum periya civapaktarkaḷ. vāli pūcitta talam kuraṅkāṭu tuṟi eṉṉum civattalam eṉappaṭukiṟatu. imayam mutal kumari variyil kōyilkaḷil civaliṅkaṅkaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. māpāratam civaliṅka vaṇakkattip paṟṟik kūṟukiṉṟatu. acuvattāmāvi aruccuṉaṉ vellum valimiyip peṟṟu avaṉ civaṉi iliṅka vaṭivil vaḻipaṭṭateṉa viyācar kūṟiyirukkiṉṟār. acuvattāmā kaṭavuḷi maṉita vaṭivil vaḻipaṭṭār.
vētaṅkaḷum upaniṭataṅkaḷum iliṅka vaṇakkattip paṟṟik kūṟukiṉṟaṉa. putiya kaṟkālak kuṭiyiruppukaḷil iliṅkaṅkaḷ kāṇap paṭṭaṉa. civaṉi iliṅka vaṭivil vaḻipaṭutal kaṟkālattilirunta teṉpatu itaṉāl terikiṟatu.
ki.pi. ēḻām nūṟṟāṇṭukku muṟpaṭṭa tamiḻ ilakkiya nūlkaḷil civaṉ eṉṉum col kāṇappaṭavilli eṉa iramaṇa cāttiri kūṟiyuḷ ḷār. 36civaṉ eṉṉum peyar vaḻakkiliruntatu. akattiyar civaṉiṭattil tamiḻik kaṟṟār. itaṉāl civaṉ tamiḻar kaṭavuḷeṉat terikiṟatu. irukku vētam iliṅka vaṇakkattik kaṇṭikkiṟatu. itaṉāl civa vaṇakkam vēta kālattukku muṉ iruntateṉat terikiṟatu. tamiḻariṉ kaṭavuḷar mali mukaṭukaḷiluṟipavar. tamiḻar kaṭavuḷ mali aracaṉ. piṟkālattil civaṉ teṉ mukakkaṭavuḷ (takkaṇāmūrtti) eṉappaṭṭār.
ākamaṅkaḷ tamiḻt toṭakka muṭiyaṉa. avi civa cittānta ñāṉattukku ātāramākavuḷḷaṉa; avi tamiḻariṉ mutirnta aṟiviṟ piṟantavi. avi makēntira maliyiliruntu civaṉāl veḷiyiṭap paṭṭavi. makēntiram tirunelvēlikkum tiruvitāṅkūrukkum iṭi yiluḷḷa potiya maliyiṉ oru cikaram. tiruvācakam civaperumāṉi “mantira māmali makēntira veṟpaṉ” “teṉ pāṇṭi nāṭṭāṉ” eṉak kūṟukiṉṟatu. civaṉ talic caṅkamirunta pulavarkaḷuḷ oruvar. iṟi vaṉik kuṟikkum paḻiya col kaṭavuḷ. uḷḷattik kaṭantavaṉ eṉpatu itaṉ poruḷ. potu makkaḷiṭiyē muḻumutal vaṇakkat tōṭu ciṟu teyva vaṇakkamum pāmpu vaṇakkamum iruntaṉa. iṉṟum aṟivu mayamāṉa tattuva ñāṉaṅkaḷōṭu mūṭa nampikkikaḷumiruntu varukiṉṟaṉa.
āriyar iṭi, kāṟṟup pōṉṟa iyaṟkip poruḷkaḷiyum iyaṟki nikaḻccikaḷiyum teyvaṅkaḷeṉak koṇṭu avaṟṟukkup paliyiṭṭu vaḻipaṭṭārkaḷ. ivvaḻipāṭu tamiḻarukkut teyva ninti pōlaviruntatu. āriyariṉ teyvaṅkaḷ tāḻntaṉavākak koḷḷap paṭṭaṉa. avi poruṭṭuc ceyyappaṭṭa vēḷvikaḷ taṭukkappaṭṭaṉa.
mikap paḻiya kālattil tamiḻar tattuvañāṉamuṭiyavarkaḷāka iruntaṉar. irukku vētakāla āriyar maṟupiṟappuk koḷkiyi aṟintirukkavilli. avarkaḷ ik koḷkiyit tamiḻariṭamiruntu aṟintārkaḷ.
tamiḻariṭiyē mutaṉ mutal koṇṭu varappaṭṭa ayalnāṭṭa var celvākku vētamatamākum. oṉṟōṭu oṉṟu campantappaṭāta camayaṅkaḷum nākarikaṅkaḷum oṉṟupaṭumpōtu eṉṉa nikaḻkiṟatu? conta vaḻipāṭum tattuva ñāṉamuṭiyavarkaḷāka irunta tamiḻa riṭiyē āriyar tamatu matattiyum tattuva ñāṉattiyum parappa muyaṉ ṟārkaḷ. vētamatam vaḻakkampōl uḷnāṭṭu vaḻakkaṅkaḷiyum camayak koḷkikaḷiyum taḻuvik koṇṭatu. tamiḻariṉ vīrat teyvaṅkaḷum (teyvaṅkaḷākkappaṭṭa vīrar) piṟateyvaṅkaḷum pirāmaṇariṉ teyvaṅkaḷākkappaṭṭaṉa. iru mataṅkaḷukkum kalappu uṇṭāyiṟṟu. tamiḻar camayattiṉ mītu ayalavar celvākkiruntatip paṟṟi nām caṅka nūlkaḷil ciṟitu aṟikiṉṟōm.
uruttiraṉ vētaṅkaḷil civaṉeṉṟu kūṟappaṭavilli eṉṟum avar puyaṟ kaṭavuḷākak kūṟappaṭṭuḷḷāreṉṟum vēta ārāycci yāḷar kūṟukiṉṟaṉar. civa eṉṉum col vētattiṟ kāṇappaṭukiṟa teṉṟum atu kaṭavuḷik kuṟiyāmal aruḷ, cāntam eṉpavaṟṟik kuṟikkiṟateṉṟum ṭākṭar pōp kūṟiyuḷḷār. vētattil civaṉeṉṉum peyar kāṇappaṭavilli eṉa ṭākṭar isṭipiṉcaṉum kāṭṭiyuḷ ḷār. uruttiraṉi akkiṉi eṉak kāṭṭa muṭiyumāyiṉum akkiṉiyi yum uruttiraṉiyum civaṉeṉak kāṭṭamuṭiyātu. uruttiraṉ oru mūrkka teyvam. atu maṟṟiya vēta teyvaṅkaḷōṭu kūṟappaṭ ṭuḷḷatu. vētaṅkaḷukkup piṟpaṭṭa kālattil atu mummūrttikaḷuḷ oṉṟāṉa civaṉākak koḷḷappaṭṭatu. uruttiraṉiyum mūrttikaḷuḷ oṉṟākak koṇṭa tamiḻar civaṉi mummūrttikaḷilum mēlāṉa kaṭavuḷākak koṇṭaṉar. itaṟku nūṟṟukkaṇakkāṉa cāṉṟukaḷit tamiḻ maṟikaḷiliruntu kāṭṭalām. “mūvar kōṉāy niṉṟa mutalvaṉ” “muḻumutalē aimpulaṉukkum mūvarkkum eṉṟaṉakkum vaḻi mutalē” eṉṟu tiruvācakam kūṟakiṉṟatu.
tamiḻariṉ civamatam vaṭanāṭṭuc celvākkukkuṭpaṭṭatu. appoḻutu tamiḻar civattuḷ vētamatattukku iṭamaḷittārkaḷ. vētattil kāṇappaṭum uruttiraṉākiya puyal kaṭavuḷip piritteṭuttu ataṟkuc civaṉukkuriya toḻilkaḷik koṭuttuc civaṉākak koṇ ṭārkaḷ. āriyar civaṉi uruttiraṉ eṉak koṇṭaṉar. ivvāṟu iṇikkappaṭṭa uruttira - civaṉ āriyar tamiḻar kaṭavuḷāka iruntār. tamiḻar teyvaṅkaḷ āriyar teyvaṅkaḷuḷ iṭam peṟṟatum civaṉ mummūrttikaḷuḷ oṉṟākkappaṭṭār. vētaṅkaḷ nāṉkākkappaṭṭa pōtu uruttiraṉ tēvarkaḷiṉ tēvaṉāka iruntār. upaniṭata kālattil vēta teyvaṅkaḷukkup patil uruttira civa vaḻipāṭu iruntatu.
avar maṅkaḷakaramāka iruntapōtu makēcuvaraṉ eṉṟum, mūrkka mākavum māmicam pucippavarākavum iruntapōtu uruttirareṉavum, ulakattik kāppavarāka irukkum pōtu makātēvareṉavum aṟiyap paṭṭār. vaḻipaṭuvōrukku vēṇṭiya citti aḷittaliṉ civaṉ eṉṉum peyaruṇṭāṉa teṉṟu māpāratam kūṟukiṉṟatu. elumpu māli aṇital mutal yōkiyākiya tōṟṟamaḷittal variyil collappaṭum civaṉiṉ vaṭivaṅkaḷ maṉitaṉiṉ aṟivu paṭippaṭiyē vaḷarcciyaṭinta kālaṅkaḷil avarkaḷ kaṭavuḷukkuk koṭuttu vaḻipaṭṭa vaṭivaṅkaḷik kuṟikkiṉṟaṉa.*
vētaṅkaḷukkum ākamaṅkaḷukku muḷḷa vēṟupāṭukaḷ
#intukkaḷiṭiyē iṉṟu naṭi muṟiyilirukkum camayamum tattuva ñāṉamum ēṟakkuṟiya muḻumiyum ākamaṅkaḷi ātāramākak koṇṭavi. ivaṟṟukkum vētaṅkaḷukkum toṭarpirukkavilli. makāpāratattukkup piṉ vitīkacamayam cīraṇamaṭiyat toṭaṅki iṉṟu muṟṟāka iṟantu viṭṭatu. ciruta kiriyikaḷiṉ perumpakuti maṟintu viṭṭatu. akkiṉi ātāṉam pōṉṟa aṟpa kiriyikaḷ mikac cilarāl ceyyappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. smārttak kiriyikaḷum virivil maṟintu koṇṭu varukiṉṟaṉa. ek kuṭumpaṅkaḷic cērntavarkaḷ mūṉṟu tali muṟikaḷ tī ōmpat tavaṟukiṟārkaḷō ak kuṭumpattiṉar pirāmaṇat taṉmiyi iḻantu viṭukiṉṟaṉar eṉṟu taruma cāttiram kūṟukiṉṟatu. iv vitiyiṉpaṭi mikaccila kuṭumpaṅkaḷiyē pirāmaṇa vakuppic cērntaṉavākak koḷḷalām. intiyā, camayatti mikap piṉpaṟṟum nāṭu. camayam ākama campantamāka irukkiṟatē aṉṟi vēta campantamāka irukka villi. vētaṅkaḷukkum ākamaṅkaḷukkumuḷḷa māṟupāṭu paḻiya kālattil naṉku aṟiyappaṭṭiruntatu. ākamak koḷkiyum vitīkak koḷkiyum etirāṉavi. cila nūṟṟāṇṭukaḷiṉ muṉ ivi oṉṟu cērkkappaṭṭaṉa. ākavē ik kālattavar iraṇṭu koḷkikaḷukku muḷḷa vēṟupāṭukaḷi uṇarāmal irukkiṉṟaṉar. ākamaṅkaḷ vētaṅ kaḷiliruntu piṟantavi eṉṟum, avi vētaṅkaḷil kūṟappaṭṭavaṟṟi viḷakka ik kālattukkēṟpac ceyyap paṭṭavi eṉṟum koḷkikaḷ nilavukiṉṟaṉa. vēta mantiraṅkaḷ tokukkappaṭṭapiṉ, avi evarā lum ceyyappaṭāmal tāmāka uḷḷaṉa eṉṉum nampikki iruntatu. ākamaṅkaḷik kaṭavuḷ kūṟiyatāka annūlkaḷ kūṟukiṉṟaṉa. vēta caṅkiti kaḷiluḷḷa mantiraṅkaḷ vitīkak kiriyikaḷil ōta vēṇṭiyavi. ākamaṅkaḷ civavaḻipāṭu tirumāl vaḻipāṭukaḷil kikkoḷḷa vēṇṭiya kiriyikaḷip paṟṟiyum, yōka cātaṉikaḷip paṟṟiyum, tattuva ñāṉaṅkaḷip paṟṟiyum kūṟukiṉṟaṉa. vētaṅkaḷ mantira pākam pirāmaṇapākam allatu kaṉma kāṇṭam ñāṉa kāṇṭam eṉa iru pakutikaḷuṭiyaṉa. ivaṟṟukku mīmāmci vēṇṭappaṭum. ākamaṅkaḷukku viḷakka urikaḷ māttiram vēṇṭappaṭum. vētaṅkaḷ cantam eṉṉum naṭiyil eḻutappaṭṭuḷḷaṉa. pāṣā eṉṉum naṭiyiṉ kālam ki.pi.1000. vitīkak kiriyikaḷ tī campantappaṭṭavi. ovvoru kiriyi yiṉ pōtum tī mūṭṭi erikkappaṭukiṟatu. tī, cuvāliyāka eriyum pōtu tēvarkaḷukku aḷikkum uṇavu cuvāliyil iṭappaṭukiṉṟatu. ākamak kiriyikaḷukkut tī vēṇṭappaṭuvatilli. uṇavu paṭikkappaṭukiṟatu. paṭikkappaṭṭa uṇaviṉ cattit teyvam āviyāka niṉṟu uṇkiṟatu; paṭittavar uṇavi eṭuttuc cuṟṟattavarukkum naṇparukkum koṭuttu uṇkiṟār. vētakkiriyikaḷil tēvarkaḷ aḻikkappaṭukiṟārkaḷ. ovvoru tēvaṉukkum pirapañcattil ovvōr atikāramuṇṭu. ākamak kiriyikaḷil oru muḻu mutaṟ kaṭavuḷē uṇṭu. avarukku paṭippu mutaliya ellā atikāraṅkaḷumuṇṭu. vētakkiriyikaḷil purōkitar puriyum ovvoru kiriyikkum vevvēṟu mantiraṅkaḷuṇṭu. cōmak koṭi koṇṭu varum vaṇṭiyil erutukaḷip pūṭṭutal, erutukaḷi ōṭṭuvataṟku kampu veṭṭutal, pali celuttum poruḷik kiyā leṭuttal, pāl kāyccutal, tayir kaṭital ivi pōṉṟa periya allatu ciṟiya kiriyikaḷ ovvoṉṟukkum pāṭal allatu vacaṉa vaṭiviluḷḷa mantiraṅkaḷ collappaṭṭaṉa. ākamakkiriyikaḷil vētamantiraṅkaḷukku iṭamilli; aṅku miṅkum cila vētamantiraṅkaḷ payaṉpaṭuttappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. avi poruttamāṉaviyalla. tū eṉat toṭaṅkum oru mantiram tūpaṅ kāṭṭumpōtu collappaṭukiṉṟatu. im mantiram vaṇṭiyiṉ nukatti uyarttuvatik kuṟikkiṉṟatu. ākamak kiriyikaḷil pōṟṟi eṉa muṭiyum tutikaḷ pāṭappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. vētak kiriyikaḷiṉ nōkkam tīyil palip poruḷkaḷi iṭuvatu. ākamak kiriyikaḷ oru aracaṉukku allatu oru viruntiṉaṉukkuc ceyvatu pōṉṟa upacāraṅkaḷic ceykiṉṟaṉa. vitīkak kiriyikaḷukkuk kaṭavuḷiṉ tiru uruvam vēṇṭappaṭavilli. tī ellāk kaṭavuḷariyum kuṟippatāka iruntatu. ākamak kiriyiyil vaḻipaṭum teyvattik kuṟikkum tiruvuruvam iṉṟiyamiyātatu.
vētattiṉ cikaram vētāntam. vētāntam eṉpatu pirapañcat tōṟṟattukkuk kāraṇamākavuḷḷa piramatti aṟintu tāṉē piramamāy piṟappi oḻippatu. ākama muṟi pattimārkkam. cariyi kiriyi yōkam ñāṉam eṉṉum paṭi muṟikaḷāl kaṭavuḷi aṭiya vēṇṭumeṉa atu kūṟukiṉ ṟatu. ākamaṅkaḷil kūṟappaṭum tattuvañāṉam vētānta ñāṉattukkup puṟam pāṉatu. vētāntam kaṭavuḷoṉṟē uḷ poruḷ eṉkiṟatu. ākamaṅkaḷil yōka mārkkam ñāṉamārkkameṉṉum pakutikaḷiruppiṉum pattimārkkamē mutaṉmi uṭiyatu.
vitīkak kiriyikaḷ makkaḷi varuṇaṅkaḷākap pirikkiṉṟatu. kaṭici varuṇattavarukku vētāntak kalvi maṟukkappaṭṭuḷḷatu. varuṇaṅkaḷiliruntu varuṇāccirama tarumaṅkaḷ vaḷarntaṉa. tuṟavu pirāmaṇarukku māttiram uriyateṉṟum, caṉṉiyācam aṉuṭṭippatāl māttiram mutti aṭiyalāmeṉṟum koḷḷappaṭṭaṉa. ākavē vitīka neṟiyiloḻukum pirāmaṇarukku māttiram mutti kikūṭum eṉak koḷḷappaṭṭatu. ākamaṅkaḷ ik koḷkiyip poruṭ paṭuttavilli; caṇṭāḷaṉāyiṉum kaṭavuḷuruvaṅkaḷi vittup pūcik kalāmeṉṟaṉa. kaṇṇappar tirukkāḷattiyil kaṭavuḷukku iṟicci vittu nivēttiyam ceytār. tirunāḷippōvār paṟik kulatti ṉar. viṇava aṭiyāruḷ oruvar pāṇa vakuppiṉar. ākamaṅkaḷ nāl varuṇak koḷkiyi aṉumatikkavilli. cūttirar vētaṅkaḷik kēṭṭal kūṭāteṉa vātarāyaṇar kūṟiyirukkiṉṟār. ākamaṅkaḷi evarum payilalām. civatīṭci peṟṟa paṟik kulattiṉaṉum pirāmaṇa ṉukkut tīṭci koṭuttu avaṉukkuk kuruvākalām. ākamak koḷki yiṉariṭiyē caṉṉiyācamum paraviyatu. viṇava caṉṉiyācikaḷ ēkānti kaḷeṉavum, civacaṉṉiyācikaḷ civayōkikaḷ eṉavum aṟiyappaṭ ṭārkaḷ. caṉṉiyācattilum pattimārkkam ciṟantateṉavum, caṉṉi yācam pattimārkkattukku vāyppu aḷippatākavum koḷḷappaṭṭaṉa.
muṟkālattil vitīkarukkum ākamak koḷkiyiṉarukkumiṭi yil veṟuppu iruntu vantatu. ākamak koḷkiyiṉar kaṭavuḷ peyarāl irattap paliyiṭuvatiyum, iṟicci uṇpatiyum - ciṟappāka māṭṭiṟicci uṇpati - vilakkiṉārkaḷ. irattappaliyiyum vēḷvi kaḷiyum paṟṟiya etiroli māpāratattil kāṇappaṭukiṉṟatu. ik kaṇṭaṉaṅkaḷiṉ palaṉāka vilaṅkukaḷip paliyiṭuvataṟkup patil māvi ṉāl ceyyappaṭṭa vilaṅkiṉuruvaṅkaḷ paliyiṭappaṭṭaṉa. pākavata matattiṉariṉ ciṟanta nūl ākamak koḷkikaḷit taḻuviya pakavatkīti. innūl vētānta ñāṉattiyum cāṅkiya ñāṉattiyum campantap paṭuttik kūṟukiṉṟatu. iññāṉaṅkaḷ oru uṇmiyi viḷakkum iru vaḻikaḷākavum ākamak karuttuṭiyaṉavākavum kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. pakavatkīti vētattiṉ karuma kaṇṭattit taḷḷukiṉṟatu. annūluḷ ākamaṅkaḷukkuriya pala paripāṭic coṟkaḷ kāṇappaṭukiṉṟaṉa.
vitīkar ākamak koḷkiyiṉari mika veṟuppuṭaṉ nōkki ṉar. vēta mantiraṅkaḷil āriyar tācukkaḷi ‘mirittiravāca’ eṉa ikaḻn tārkaḷ. av vikaḻcciyiṉ toṭarpē vitīkar ākamikariṭam kāṭṭiya veṟuppākum. yamuṉāccāriyar kālam mutal vitīkak koḷkikaḷum ākamak koḷkikaḷum iṇikkappaṭṭapōtum iṉṟum av veṟuppi nām kāṇalām. vētāntikaḷ, civa viṇava ālayaṅ kaḷil pūci ceyyum pirāmaṇari maṟṟiya pirāmaṇarilum tāḻntava rākak karutuvar. aimpatu āṇṭukaḷiṉ muṉṉum atvita vētāntikaḷ kōyilkaḷuḷ nuḻiyātiruntamiyi yām aṟivōm. vētattiṉ ciracu eṉappaṭum vētāntam ākamattik kaṇṭikkiṟatu. vātarāyaṇar pācupatattiyum pāñcarāttirattiyum kaṇṭittirukkiṟār.
āriyariṉ vētaṅkaḷ tōṉṟumuṉ tācukkaḷiṉ matam vaṭa nāṭṭilum teṉṉāṭṭilumiruntatu. ciruta kiriyikaḷ pirāmaṇar, aracar, purōkitarukku atika takkaṇi koṭukkakkūṭiya celvam paṭitta vaṇikarukku māttiram uriyaṉavāyiruntaṉa; potu makkaḷ tamatu contak kiriyikaḷi uṭiyavarkaḷāka iruntārkaḷ. ak kiriyikaḷ tācukkaḷiṉ kiriyikaḷāka iruntaṉa. avi iṉṟu cāntāl makkaḷiṭiyē kāṇappaṭuvaṉapōl teyvattukku uṇavu paṭittal āṭutal pāṭutal vakikaḷiliruntaṉa. vālmīkar cukkirīpaṉiṉ muṭi cūṭṭip paṟṟik kūṟiyiruppatu itaṉi viḷakkukiṉṟatu.
makāpāratattiṉ piṉ āriyariṉ tī vaḻipāṭu vīḻcci aṭintatu. pirāmaṇariṉ pārvi naṭimuṟiyilirunta kiriyikaḷil ceṉṟatu. avarkaḷ pirāmaṇaṅkaḷip patti vaḻiyil tiruppiṉārkaḷ; tirumūrtti eṉṉum koḷkiyit tōṟṟuvittārkaḷ; cāṅkiyattil kūṟappaṭum mukkuṇattit tirumūrttikaḷōṭu toṭarpu paṭuttiṉārkaḷ. ciṟitu ciṟitāka 108 viṇava ākamaṅkaḷiyum 28 civa ākamaṅkaḷiyum ceytapiṉ 77 cakti ākamaṅkaḷiyum ceytārkaḷ. pāṇiṉi muṉivar civa vaḻipāṭṭiyum kiruṭṭiṇa vaḻipāṭṭiyum kuṟippiṭṭirukkiṉṟār. 
vētāntamum ākamamum mika metuvāka iṇintu koṇṭu vantaṉa. purāṇaṅkaḷil avi oṉṟiṉ pakkattil oṉṟāka varukiṉṟaṉa; oṉṟāka iṇiyavilli; caṅkarāccāriyar kālattilum avi iṇiyāmalē iruntaṉa. avar vātarāyaṇarip piṉpaṟṟi pācupata pāñcarāttira mataṅkaḷip puṟac camayaṅkaḷeṉak koḷkiṉṟār. caṅkarar ceyta pirapañca irutayam eṉpatu ākamattit taḻuviya nūl. avar caṭmata tāpaṉācāriyar eṉappaṭṭār. avar viṣṇu, civaṉ, catti, kaṇapati, cuppiramaṇiyar, cūriyaṉ eṉṉum vaḻipāṭukaḷit tām toṭaṅkiya maṭaṅkaḷil ēṟpaṭuttiṉār.
viciṭṭāttuvitam eṉṉum viṇava vētāntatti toṭaṅkiya yamuṉāccāriyar viṇava ākamaṅkaḷi vētaṅkaḷip pōlap piramāṇamākka vēṇṭumeṉak kaṭṭaḷiyiṭṭu iraṇṭiyum oṉṟu cērttār.
camakkiruta ātikkam
teṟkē vitīka matam paravat toṭaṅkiṟṟu. vitīka nūlkaḷ camak kirutattil eḻutappaṭṭiruntaṉa. teṉṉāṭṭavar camakkirutam payiṉṟaṉar. pāṇiṉi muṉivarukkup piṉ ciṟanta vaṭamoḻi nūlkaḷic ceytavarkaḷ perumpālum teṉṉāṭṭiṉarākavē kāṇappaṭukiṉ ṟaṉar.37 apastampar, pōtāyaṉar, kuṭaliyar, kāttiyāyaṉar, kumārilar, vaṟcayāyaṉar, cāyaṇar, caṅkarar, irāmāṉucar, mātavar, vittiyāraṇiyar mutaliya teṉṉāṭṭiṉar ceyta vaṭamoḻi nūlkaḷ pukaḻpeṟṟu viḷaṅkukiṉṟaṉa. purāṇaṅkaḷ palavaṟṟic ceytavarkaḷum teṉṉāṭṭiṉarē.
pallavarum avarukkup piṉ vanta vaṭanāṭṭu araca parampari yiṉarum camakkirutattukkup pērātaravu aḷittārkaḷ. pirāmaṇar vāḻum iṭaṅkaḷ tōṟum kaṭikikaḷ allatu piramapurikaḷ eṉṉum camakkirutak kalācālikaḷ niṟuviṉārkaḷ. avikaḷil kalvi payilum māṇavarukkum kalvi payiṟṟum āciriyarukkum uṇavu uṭi mutaliyaṉa vaḻaṅkiṉar. kalā cālikaḷil vētaṅkaḷ, vētāṅkaṅkaḷ, taruma cāttiraṅkaḷ, arttacāttiram mutaliya kalvikaḷ kaṟpikkappaṭṭaṉa. camakkirutak kalvi pirāmaṇariṉ ēkapōka urimiyāka iruntatu. kaṭikikaḷil kaṟṟut tēṟiya pirāmaṇar irācakurukkaḷ eṉṉum peyaruṭaṉ nāṭu muḻumiyilum ceṉṟu vitīka matatti makkaḷukkup pōtittārkaḷ. irāca kurukkaḷē araca kuṭumpattiṉarukkuk kalvi kaṟpittārkaḷ.*
pirāmaṇariṉ cēvi vēṇṭappaṭṭa iṭaṅkaḷil avarkaḷ ceṉṟu vāḻvataṟkut tūṇṭutalāka nilamum vīṭum māṉiyamāka vaḻaṅkappaṭṭaṉa. ivvāṟu vitīkattukkum camakkirutattukkum cel vākku vaḷarntu koṇṭu ceṉṟatu. camaya campantamāṉavi ellām camakkirutattil iruttal vēṇṭum. camakkirutattukku atikārikaḷ pirāmaṇar eṉpavi pōṉṟa karuttukkaḷ nāḷ vītam palamaṭintu koṇṭu vantaṉa. ākavē, tamiḻil camayacampantamāṉa tala purāṇaṅ kaḷō, vēṟu purāṇaṅkaḷō eḻutuvōrum tām eḻutuvaṉa ētō vaṭamoḻi nūliluḷḷaṉa eṉak kūṟum vaḻakku ēṟpaṭṭatu. camakkirutat tiliruntu tāṉ ulakiluḷḷa ellā moḻikaḷum tōṉṟiṉa. am moḻiyilillāta aṟivu vēṟetilumilli eṉavum kūṟappaṭṭaṉa.38 pallavarum avarukkup piṟpaṭṭa aracarum tamiḻk kalviyiṉ poruṭṭu ātaravaḷittatip paṟṟiya kalveṭṭuc cācaṉam oṉṟēṉum kāṇap paṭavilli. kalvi eṉpatu camakkirutak kalvi oṉṟumē eṉak karutap paṭṭatu. camakkirutak kalā cālikaḷil ākamaṅkaḷ payilappaṭṭatākak kūṟappaṭavilli. vitīkar ākamaṅkaḷiyum, vētaṅkaḷiyum vētat tōṭu campantappaṭṭa nūlkaḷiyum pōl ciṟantaṉavāka matikka villi. kōyil pūci ceyyum pirāmaṇar ēṉiya pirāmaṇarilum tāḻntavarkaḷāka nōkkappaṭṭaṉar.*
civa maṭaṅkaḷ
40tamiḻ nāṭṭil vitikam campantam peṟāta civa maṭaṅka ḷiruntaṉa. avaṟṟil kuravariṭattil mahṇahkkar pāṭaṅkēṭṭal camaya cātaṉikaḷ ceytal pōṉṟa nikaḻccikaḷ naṭipeṟṟaṉa. kōyilkaḷ pirāmaṇariṉ kikku māṟiyapōtu kōyilkaḷukkup pakkattil maṭaṅka ḷamikkappaṭṭaṉa. kōyili mēṟpārkkum pirāmaṇar maṭattiliruntu kōyil kiriyikaḷ oḻuṅkāka naṭipeṟuvatik kavaṉittu vantār. ivvāṟiruntu varumpōtu pirāmaṇarallātavar tuṟavikaḷāvataṟkum (caṉṉiyācam koḷvataṟkum) avarkaḷ maṭaṅkaḷukkut talivarāva taṟkum taṭi eḻuntatu. ākavē, pirāmaṇarallāta tuṟavikaḷ kukikaḷi nāṭic ceṉṟaṉar. pirāmaṇarallātāriṉ kuki maṭaṅkaḷ atikappaṭṭu avaṟṟiṉ celvākkum atikappaṭṭa pōtu ammaṭaṅkaḷi aḻittut tarimaṭṭappaṭuttumpaṭi pirāmaṇar tammi ātarippōrit tūṇṭiṉar.41 ‘kuki iṭi kalakam’ eṉṉum peyaril periya kalakaṅkaḷ nērntaṉa. kuki iṭi kalakaṅkaḷippaṟṟic cācaṉaṅkaḷ kūṟukiṉṟaṉa. pirāmaṇarallātāriṉ maṭaṅkaḷ aḻittut tarimaṭṭamākkappaṭṭaṉa. mūṉṟāṅ kulōttuṅka cōḻaṉ kālattil pirāmaṇa matattavar pirāmaṇa rallātāriṉ maṭamoṉṟukkuk koṭutta cottu piṭuṅkappaṭṭatip paṟṟi oru cācaṉaṅ kūṟukiṉṟatu. vicaya nakara aracar kālattil pirāmaṇa rallātār tuṟavu pūṇuvataṟku etirāṉa vaḻakkoṉṟu nērntatu, appoḻutu vicaya nakara aracariṉ kīḻ atikāriyāka irunta ciṉṉa cevvappa nāyakkar av vaḻakkukkut tīrppaḷikkum paṭi civākkira yōkikaḷik kēṭṭukkoṇṭār. avar tamatu tīrppi ‘civacamaya caṉṉiyāca pattati’ eṉṉum nūl vaṭivil kūṟiṉār. atu pirāmaṇa rallātārukku aṉu kūlamāṉatu.
kōyilkaḷ pirāmaṇar kippaṭṭapiṉ iṉṉoru koḷki yum tali eṭuttatu. camaya aṟivi vētaṅkaḷiliruntu nērē aṟivatallatu uḷ nāṭṭu moḻikaḷil eḻutappaṭṭa nūlkaḷik kaṟṟu avi mūlam aṟivatāl payaṉilli eṉṉum koḷki eḻuntatu. vaṭamoḻik kalvi pirāmaṇarukku māttiram ēka pōka urimiyāka iruntatu. 42ik koḷkiyit tamiḻaṟiñar etirttaṉar. viṇavaril teṉkaliyiṉar itaṟkut talicāykkavilli. ak kālattil tamiḻ maṟumalarcci peṟṟatu. uriyāciriyarkaḷ tōṉṟip paḻantamiḻ nūlkaḷukku urikaḷ ceytaṉar. cantāṉa kuravarkaḷ camaya nūlkaḷit tamiḻil ceytaṉar. cittar nūlkaḷum ik kālatti aṭuttu eḻuntaṉa. cittar nūlkaḷ pirāmaṇa ātikkatti etirkka eḻuntavi. civa maṭaṅkaḷ pala tōṉṟiṉa. civa maṭaṅkaḷiṉ talivar pirāmaṇarallātārākavē iruntu varuvar.
pirāmaṇar kōyilkaḷukkut talivarāṉa pōtu kōyil peyarkaḷ vaṭamoḻippaṭuttappaṭṭaṉa. tirumaṟikkāṭu vētāraṇiya meṉavum, mutukuṉṟu viruttācalam eṉavum, kuṭamūkku kumpakōṇameṉa vum, veṇkāṭu cuvētavaṉa meṉavum, tiruppukalūr caraṇayapuram eṉavum, tiruviyāṟu pañcanatam eṉavum paṭṭaṉa.
kōyilkaḷ toṭarpākac cācaṉaṅkaḷil kāṇappaṭum cila peyarkaḷ; taḷiccēri - kōyilic cūḻnta kuṭiyiruppu; kaṟṟaḷi-kaṟ kōyil; naṭṭuvaṉ, aṇṇāvi naṭaṉaṅ kaṟṟuk koṭuppōr; āṭuvār; kaṉapāṭi; mukavīṇikkārar; uṭukki vācikkiṟavar; vīṇi vācip pōr; āriyam pāṭuvār; tamiḻ pāṭuvār; koṭṭi mattaḷak kārar; muttiri caṅku ūtuvōr; pakka vāttiyakārar; kaṭṭiyaṅkūṟu vōr; mēḷam vācippavar; kāntaruvar; viḷakkuppōṭukiṟavar; nīr teḷippavar; eṭupiṭi cāmāṉ tūkkukiṟavarkaḷ; vaṇṇāṉ; nāvitaṉ; kollaṉ; tiyāṉ; pāṭukiṟavaṉ; cōtiṭaṉ; kaṉṉāṉ; ōccaṉ; taṭṭāṉ; pāṇaṉ; kaṇakkaṉ.
vitīkattukku etirppu
caṅka kālattiṟuti mutal cila nūṟṟāṇṭukaḷ putta camaṇa mataṅkaḷ teṟkil celvākkup peṟṟiruntaṉa. ki.pi. 5 ām nūṟṟāṇṭil vaccira nanti eṉṉum camaṇa muṉivariṉ talimiyil maturiyil ōr tamiḻc caṅkam iruntatu. ic caṅkattilēyē patiṉeṇkīḻkkaṇakkic cērnta nūlkaḷ pala ceyyappaṭṭaṉa veṉṟu karutappaṭukiṉṟaṉa. tiruñāṉa campantar kālattuk kūṉ pāṇṭiyaṉum, appar cuvāmikaḷ kālattil pallavamāṟavarmaṉum camaṇa matattit taḻuviyiruntārkaḷ. māṇikkavācaka cuvāmikaḷ puttarōṭu vātuceytu veṉṟatākap purāṇam kūṟukiṉṟatu. putta camaṇa mataṅkaḷ celvākkup peṟ ṟirunta kālattu civarum viṇava camayattavarum oruṅku cērntu putta camaṇa mataṅkaḷi etirttārkaḷ. vitīka camayattiṉarum ivar kaḷuṭaṉ cērntaṉar. appoḻutu vitīkar ākamak koḷkikaḷ pala vaṟṟit taḻuviṉar; tamatu vētaṅkaḷ civa viṇava camayaṅkaḷum mutal nūlkaḷeṉṟaṉar. ikkoḷki peyaraḷaviliruntataṉṟic ceyalaḷavi lirukkavilli. vētaṅkaḷum ākamaṅkaḷum māṟupaṭṭaṉaveṉṉum koḷki iruntu vantatu. vētaṅkaḷum ākamaṅkaḷum māṟupaṭṭavi yalla eṉap piṟkālattavar kūṟivantaṉar. piṟkālattavarkaḷ vētam eṉak kūṟiyavaṟṟi nōkkiṉāl avi vētaṅkaḷik kuṟiyātu piṟkāla upa niṭataṅkaḷik kuṟippaṉavākat terikiṉṟaṉa. itaṉi civañāṉa muṉivariṉ civañāṉa pōtamā pāṭiyattil āṅkāṅku kūṟappaṭuvaṉa vaṟṟik koṇṭu naṉku uyttaṟiyalām.
kōyilkaḷil vitīkar talimi eytutaliyum aṅku āriyam pāṭappaṭuvatiyum aṟiñar etirttuk kiḷarcci ceytārkaḷ. “āriyaṉ kaṇṭāy tamiḻaṉ kaṇṭāy” “centamiḻōṭu āriyaṉic cīriyāṉi” “āriyan tamiḻō ṭiciyāṉavaṉ” eṉat tirunāvukkaracu nāyaṉār tamatu tiruppāṭalkaḷil kūṟi irucārāriyum cantu ceytār. “āriyap puttakap pēy koṇṭu pulampiṟṟu” eṉa nakkīrar tām pāṭiya kōpap piracāttil vaṭamoḻip pāṭalkaḷip pāṭutali veṟuttuk kūṟukiṉṟār.
tolkāppiyap poruḷatikāra uriyil (poruḷ 490)
āriya naṉṟu tamiḻ tīteṉa vuritta
kāriyattāṟ kālakkōṭ paṭṭāṉic - cīriya
antaṇ potiyil akattiyaṉā rāṇiyāl
centamiḻē tīrkka cuvākā.
eṉṉum veṇpā oṉṟu mēṟkōḷākak kāṭṭappaṭṭuḷḷatu. ak kālattil āriyam tamiḻ eṉpavaṟṟukku iṭiyilirunta māṟupāṭu kaḷi iv veṇpā uṇarttukiṉṟatu.

NOTES
(Quotations from eminent authors in support of the statements found in this book)
1. The original home of the Indo-Germanic language was the long stretch of grass-land extending from the north of the Carpathians and the Lower Danube to the foot-hills below Alti and Tianshan in Central Asia skirting the shores of the Black Sea and Caspian, and extending south to Cacasus and the steep north edge of Persia. This was the area of characterization of a race of tall, fair-skinned, blue-eyed, narrow-headed giants to whom the name Proto-Nodics has been given. The grass-land made them develop a pastoral life, modified by some hunting on the one hand and some very primitive agriculture on the other. Their one noteable contribution to the growth of world civilization was that the domesticated horse.
About 2,500 B.C., a great wave of descciation seems to have passed over Asia which converted steppes of the north as well as the Semites of Arabian grass-land in search of pastures new. This great displacement of tribes included the “Ganaanite” invasion of Syria referred to in the Genesis as the Semite migration into Mesapotamia leading to the establishment of a powerful Babylonian monarchy. From the northern steppes, the Nordics went out in many branches. - The age of the mantras pp. 103, 105. - P.T.S. Iyengar.
2. Pargiter adduces considerable evidence to show that the true Brahman families were of pre-Rigvedic origin, and the Aryan kings of Madhya Desa were their own priests in the earliest times had no Brahmans. - Castes in India its nature, function and origins. – J.H.Hutton.
3. The language of the Rig-Veda is as yet purely Aryan or Indo-European in its form, structure and spirit but its phonetics is already affected by the Dravidian and it has already begun to borrow words from Dravidian and Kol. Among the words of probable Dravidian origin in the Rig-Veda the following may be noted.
anu – particle; arani – rubbing wood for fire; kapi – monkey; karmara – smith; kala – time; kunda – hole; gana – band; nana – several; nila – blue; pushpa – flower; puja – worship; pala – fruit; majura – peafowl; ratri – night; rupa – form. - The origin and development of Bengali p.42. - S.K. Chaterji.
4. … the aboriginal Dravidian culture which certinly assimilated by them, and may thus be considered as their inheritance lending itself to more convenient consideration as part and parcel of our Vedic heritage rather than as distinct from it. - Hindu view in art. p. 9 – Maluk Raj Anand (Asia Publishing house, 1957).
5. The whole of the Veda, Sruti (heard or revealed was compiled during the long period from about 1,500 B.C. to 500 B.C.) and includes the following extensive literature: (1) The four Vedas proper Rig, Yajur, Sama, Atharva which are hymns, prayers, and sacred formulas offered by priests to the gods on behalf of rich lay-sacrificers, charms for witchcraft, medicine and other homely practices, manipulated by magicians and medicine men in min for the pliner people. - Ibid p. 10.
5. The authors of the hymns, called Rishis, composed them for the purpose of invoking the help of gods in events that immediately interested them to secure success in impending battles (R.V. XIX – 4), to avert drought (R.V.68), to help to rise crops (A.V.VI. 142) to enable them to live a “hundred autums” till their sons became fathers in their turn (R.V.I. 89. 9), to satisfy all possible wants (A.V.XV.9), and to escape all kinds of dangers and difficulties (A.V.XIX.7) - The age of the mantras p.4. - P.T.S. Iyengar.
6. The shock of intercourse with the alien culture of the Dravidians awaked in the conquerors the desire to preserve their literary inheritance, and although during the time it took to give it a permanent shape it became strongly mixed with aboriginal Dravidian belief, this was the way that the Vedas, the oldest books of the Hindus came to be composed. - Hindu view of art p. 10. – Maluk Raj Anand.
7. Of the writings called Anukramani in which the metre, the deity and author of each song are given in their proper order. - The history of Indian literature p. 61. - A Weber.
8. Of the gods invoked in the Vedas the following are chief. Dyus or Dyus Pitar, sky or father of sky; Surya and Savitir, Vishnu, the sun-god; ushas the dawn; Agni the fire; Pritivi the earth; Soma, the intoxicating vegetable juice used in ritual; Indra the god of lightning and thunder; Varuna the universal embracer and encompasser; Adityas, boundless ones; Asvins, horse men; Vayu, the wind; Rudra, the fierce god of distruction and waste etc. This list was considerably enlarged as the Aryans continued to assimilate the gods and goddnesses of the non-Aryan inhabitants of India. - Hindu view in art. – p.11.
9. Civa is a god unknown to the Vedas; his name is a word of not frequent occurrence in the hymns, indeed but means simply prosperous, not even in the Atharvan it is the epithet of a particular divinity or distinguished by the usage, from any other adjectives. The precise relation between Civa and Rudra is not yet satisfactorily traced out. - Oriental linguistic studies. P.30. - William Dwlight Whitney.
10. Practically no traces of it (rebirth) are to be found in the Vedas or in the poems of Homer. The Vedic hero like the Homeric hero goes to dwell in the Elysium of Yama, the proto-man, and returns no more to earth. - India and the Western World. - H.G. Rawlinson.
10. The doctrine of transmigration is entirely absent from the Vedas and early Brahmanas. It seems probable that the Indian Aryans borrowed the idea from the aboriginals. - Cambridge History of India, p. 108. - Prof. Macdonald.
11. The simple ritual of the Rig-Veda had now under the influence of Dravidian methods of worship, became an elaborate system of mechanical rites and ceremonies in Brahmanas. - Hindu view in art. p. 18.
… although the religion of the Rig-Veda hymns (composed before the Hindus crossed the Satlej) owed nothing to Indian aboriginal influence, the same is not true of later Samhitas and Brahmanas. - The riddles of Mohenjo-daro. - G.R. Hunter – New Review Vol.3, p. 314.
12. During the Brahmana period we notice the beginning of the regular worship of Siva … in this period Sivan or Rudra gradually become to be one of the most important figures of the reformed Indo-Aryan pantheon. - Pre-historic ancient and Hindu India, p.43 – R.D. Banerji.
The worship of Siva or Mahadeva towards the close of this period … the deity being identified with Rudra of the Vedic poets, the howling god of tempests and the father of Maruts. - The philosophy of the Upanishads, p. 18 – A. Edward Gough.
13. The transference of the same Soma to the moon which appears in the later history of Indian religion, is hitherto-obscure; the Vedas hardly know it neither do they seem to prepare the way for it - Oriental and linguistic studies, p.10 – William Dwlight Whitney.
14. The cult of the Linga is older than the Calcolithic period of Mohenjo – Daro will be evident if we only take back our research into the domin of pre-historic archeology. It seems probable that these pre-Aryan phallic worshippers are identical with the peoples who in later times dwelt in the Indus valley, and prejudice and indignation aginst whom find most eloquent expressions in the following two passages of the Rig-Veda - Pre-aryan elements in Indian Culture – K. Sur. - Indian Historical Journal 1934.
15. The vowel system of Vedic language is much simpler and its consonant system more developed than those of the parent Indo-Germanic or of its European branches. A large portion of the vocabulary of the Vedic tongue is not found in the allied languages and must have been picked up in India; and even in matters of syntax and sentence-structure it underwent special developments in Indian soil. - The age of the Mantras – p. 4.
The Dravidian dialects effected profoundly the sounds, the structure, the idiom and the vocabulary of the former and the differences already alluded to between Vedic language and its hypothetic parent, called or its European decendants, Greek, Latin, etc., are due to the influence of the Dravidian dialects of India. In the course of its growth in India, on account of the constant influence of Dravidian tongues, this language lost the subjunctive mood, many infinitive forms and several noun declensions, forgot its richly varied system of real verb tenses and adopted turns of expressions peculiar to the Dravidian idiom. - Ibid, p.6.
The Dravidian names of things and operations connected with all these arts of peace are native and not foreign (i.e., borrowed from Sanskrit). The question has not yet been investigated, but on enquiry it will most probably turn out that many Sanskrit words connected with these arts were borrowed from the Dravidian.
It is not surprising, therefore, that this Indo-Germanic language was profoundly affected when it spread among the people of ancient India, that it shed some of its vowels, Indo-Germanic a,e,o all being leveled down to one uniform a, that it developed new consonants, e.g., the sibilants, s’, s, sh, hopelessly confused in the pronunciation of Sanskrit in various parts of India and that its grammar was slowly but surely modified. - Ibid p. 15.
16. All other Vedic gods (1) Savita, Pusha, Vayu, Surya, Ushas, the Maruts, Soma and Yama (2) Varuna, Rudra, Tvashta and Aditi (3) Brahaspathi, Prajapati, Skamba and Bramhanaspati are all purely Indian deities. Of these, the first group seems to have been evolved from germs of ideas brought along the current of the Indo-Germanic dialect that evolved into the language of the Mantras. The etymology of most of these names is plin, but deities corresponding to them in name and function are not found outside India. The gods of the second group seem to have been taken over from the Dravidian-speaking tribes of India. It has been already pointed out that the Dravidian languages profoundly affected the Vedic language, similarly the gods worshipped by the tribes that gradually accepted this language must have been “Aryanized” and adopted the Vedic pantheon. Those Vedic gods the etymology of whose names is not patent and who have no analogues in other Indo – Germanic dialects must have been Indian gods to whom such treatment was accorded. - Ibid pp. 123, 4.
17. Brahmanas contin discussions on both work and knowledge. Those sections of the Brahmanas which contin symbolic or spiritual discussions on both ‘work and knowledge are called Aranyakas, for these were read in the aranya (woods, forest) becuse owing to the obtruse character, they were not imparted everywhere to everybody indiscriminately’ and becuse great seclusion was needed for their comprehension. Many of the Upanishads are included among the Aranyakas; only one Upanishad is included in mantras or Samhita Viz., in Isopanishad which forms the last (fortieth) chapter of the white Yajur Veda. – What are the Upanishads? – Indo Asian Culture Vol.1 p. 53 (1952).
18. Indications intimate that the real guardians of these thoughts were not originally the priestly caste, absorbed in the ceremonial, but rather the caste of the Kshatriyas. Agin and agin in the Upanishads we meet the situation that the Brahman begs the Kshatrya for instruction which the latter after several representations of the unseemliness of such a proceeding imparts to him. – The system of Vedanta. Dr. Paul Deussen.
18. Another meaning of the word Upanishad is mystery becuse its teachings or contents are not revealed or imparted to anybody or everybody at any place or every place without discrimination. That is how the two words Upanishad and mystery came to be synonimus. How great a mystery the Upanishads were supposed to be gathered from this that they were not tught to any one except the eldest son or the most favourite pupil even for the gift of world kingdom – What are the Upanishads – Indo-Asian Culture Vol.1 p.53.
18. The oral methods of communication was held all the more sacred as we find in the ancient priesthood, whose ritual and gnosis depend on the living memory for their truth and sanctity. It was the mode of communication from mouth to ear combined in all the mysteries including masonry – Nature Genesis Vol.2 p. 10 – Gerald Massay.
18. On the grounds indicated above, we may infer the Upanishadic speculations originated wholly outside the pale of Vedic Brahmanism and had their source in the religio – philosophical thought currents already prevalent in India since Pre-aryan days. That a rich culture which had been flourishing in India for at least two millena before the advent of the Vedic Aryans, should produce philosophical thinking and religious ideas of refined types is no difficult to make, for, it is but normal to expect this evolution – the pre-Vedic elements constituted the texture while the Vedic did probably no more than to imprint the stamp Upanishads.
It would be historically more correct, therefore, to regard Upanishadic as much as Jaina and Buddhist thought as having their roots more in non-Vedic than in Vedic ideas. We also find the basic ideas of the Samkhya and Yoga permiate Jaina, Buddhist as well as the Upanishadic outlook and it is probable that the primitive Samkhya consisted the philosophical back ground par excellence of pre-Vedic Indian thought and Yoga consisted an essential element in the cultivation of matters concerning the spirit. Both Samkhya and Yoga had developed probably already in pre-Aryan India …, the origin of Upanishads was not at all Vedic. We must not forget the priestly classes and philosophical thinkers with their religious practices and ideas who existed in India from before the coming of the Indian Aryans. By Buddha’s time they have probably been absorbed in the part of the Vedic society and came to be called Brahmans – Back ground of Buddhist Philosophy – Prof. Dr. B.B. Bhattacharia M.A.D. Ph.D. – Indo Asian Culture No.1.
Upanishads (Skt. upa – unto, ni – down, sad – to sit and so literally a sitting down by, sitting one self at the feet of another, confidential communication, esoteric doctrine) With the Aranyakas the oldest speculative treatise of the Hindus; they lie at the root of the philosophical side of Hinduism equally with the mantras and Brahmanas, but they are practically the only Veda of all educated Hindus at the present day. Properly each Brahmana had its Aranyakas, or forest treatise, intended for the Vanaprasthas, or dwellers in the forest (that is Brahman who having passed the two earlier stages of the bramacharin, or student and grihastha or householder retire into the forest, to devote themselves to self mortification and religious meditations); but the mythical doctrines of the latter were so mingled with extraneous matter that the chapters called Upanishads appear to have been added to investigate more exclusively and definitely such problems as the origin of the universe, the nature of deity, the nature of soul and the connection of spirit and matter. Some of the most important are the Aitareya Upanishad and Kaushitakibrahmana Upanishad of Rigveda; the Taittriya belonging the Taittriya samhita of the Yajur Veda; the Brihadaranyaka attached to the Shatapathabrahmana of Vajasaneyisanhitha of that Veda and the Isha or Ishavasya, forming the 40th Chapter of the latter sanhita; the Chandogya and Kena belonging to the Sama Veda, and Prasana, Mundaka, Mandukya and Katha belong to the atharvaveda. Following the stratificatory principle in general the only guide in determining the age of Sanskrit works, the ancient Upanishads – that of those which occupy a place in the Sankitas, Brahmanas and Aranyakas – are believed to be older than 600 B.C. or anterior to Buddhism though the germs of the doctrines contined in them are to be in some of the latest hymns. The others range through long period, and very numerous. The ancient vedic-literature first became known outside India through these Upanishads. - The century encyclopedia of names.
18. Dravidian Pandits composed some Upanishads and Brahmanas and why not Vedas Upanishads and Darsanas; six schools each with its text book and sutra sundry, Brahmanas and philosophies, theistical and atheistical, all of which preceded Buddah, and were founded by Kapila a quasi divine incarnation of Vishnu, but in reality a stolid Dravidian Pandit – Short Studies in the science of comparative Religions p. 250 – Forlong.
18. In a word we may say that as we pass from the Vedas to Upani-shads, we pass from prayer to philosophy from hymnology to reflections, from polytheism to monotheistic mysticism – Constructive Survey of Upanishadic Philosophy p. 3 – R.D. Ranade.
18. In the Upanishads however we find no only kings but also women and even people of dubious descent taking part in the literary philosophical aspirations of the highest knowledge – The History of Indian literature p. 220 – Winternitz.
Upanishadic age to have been placed somewhere between 1,200 B.C. and 600 B.C. Ibid – p. 13.
19. Two of them (Darsanas) are wholly based on the Vedic texts and are called the two Mimamsas; they are Purva and Uttara otherwise Karma mimamsa and Brahma mimamsa, investigation of Dharma and of Brahma. The other four are based on reasoning and while paying homage to the supreme authority of the Veda do not derive their substance from Vedic texts viz., Sankhya, Yoga, Nyaya and Vaiseshika the disciplines of enumeration effort reasoning and definition respectively – Outlines of Indian Philosophy. P. 2 – P.T.S. Iyengar.
20. There is one passage only in which decided by hostile feeling towards the Brahmanic priest-hood may be discovered in Kapila’s sutras and it seems full of meaning. Among the different kinds of bondage to which men are liable but ought not to be, is one called Dakshina banda, bondage rising having to offer gifts to priests which seems to be condemned as superstitious and mischievous – Indian Philosophy – Max-Muller
21. Among the innumerable Purushas that are in the world there is one called Isvara. The mention of Isvara in the Yoga sutras has made many people describe the Yoga as a school of theism; but this is extremely inaccurate; for the Isvara mentioned in the Yoga is in no sense God. He is neither the ruler of nature nor the moral governor of the Universe. Out of the multitude of Purushas in the Universe, he is a special Purusha who was never touched by Klesa, the defects of ignorance, egoism, desire, aversion, and clinging of life, and by the mental deposits left by Karma and their fruition. In Him is fully developed the seed of omniscience which every Purusha has. He is the ancient teacher whose life is unbroken by time as ours is. The Isvara of Yoga Darsana, therefore, is neither the reality behind nature, nor any universal being which human selves find their unity. Except omniscience and mastery over time, he has no other divine attribute, His only function being that of an ancient teacher. Hence Yoga is in its tenets as atheistic as Sankya … For the Isvara here referred to is not the lord of the world, but the lord of his devotee, and He is his lord only in the sense that he figures Him in the heart as the mystic syllable ‘Om’ and this makes it easy for him to reach his own inner consciousness – Outlines of Indian Philosophy pp. 115, 116.
22. According to Haribadra’s Shaddarsanasamuchchaya Gautama and Kanada founders respectively of Nyaya and Vaiseshika systems, were of Saiva persuation. Ganaratna, in his commentary of Haribadra’s work says that the Naiyayikas were called Saivas and the Vaiseshikas, Pasupathas among the successors of Asoka we come across one Galanka who was a Saiva – The History and Culture of Indian People Vol.2 p. 456.
23. The Vedanta was a great reformation which began at least four centuries B.C. when Buddhism had obtined a firm hold in upper India … It is clearly a Dravidian reformation of the crude Aryan elemental teaching, a building up of a new - Hindusm purified by the ancient Turano philosophic schools of Kapila and embracing the piety and ethics of the followers of the great Jaina sint Mahavira and his probable disciple Sakya muni – Short Studies in the Science of Comparative Religions. P 265.
Dravidians as we many conveniently designate the great rulers of India then, and from 2,000 to 3,000 B.C. Long expected evidence is now appearing that they – Dravid pandits composed some Upanishads and Brahmanas and why not Vedas, engrafting there is the hymns prayers and faith of illiterate Aryans? All these scriptures are inferior and easy compositions to philosophical works which issued from the schools of Kapila before Buddah’s day there was or any Aryan settlement in the middle Ganges. Nor would Vedic compositions prove difficult to learned Dravidian Brahmans e.g. Apastamba to Sangaracharya 800 A.D. who wrote on complicated philosophies of the Vedanta, the Bashya or Commentaries on the Sutras and Upanishads –aphorisms and hymns which are all still the admiration of even European metaphysicians, thosophists and most pious thinkers. - Short studies in the Science of Comparative Religions, p. 241.
24. The teachings of the Bhagavad Gita have suffered more than those of any other Indian book from the hands of the commentator. It is not cryptic in style like the sutras; but yet, from the great veneration pid to it on accounts of its supposed authorship and on account of its real superiority to every other scripture Indian or non-Indian, so many Bashyakaras have attempted to use it for butteressing up their special theories and expended their tender mercies on it. Its teachings and its locutions technical or otherwise have been violently tampered with by the commentators who did not possess what we call a literary conscience. The commentator did not aim to discover what exactly his author thought or attempted to express, but used the text for supporting his own special theories. If any passages were inconveniently opposed to the commentator’s theories, they were to be explined away by utalizing grammatical and etymological tricks - Outlines of Indian Philosophy. P. 246.
25. The original event Mahabharata seems to be a non-Aryan one, if we judge from the blood thirst of Bhima, the polyandry of Drupada and such other incidents, but it was soon converted into an Aryan story. - Indian Philosophy Vol.II, p.479. - Prof. S. Radhakrishnan.
26. Sayana in his commentary on the Black Yajur Veda says that the Mahabharata and the Puranas are designed to teach the law of duty to women and the sudras who were not allowed to read the Vedas. - Ibid. Vol.II, p. 452.
27. This event, it appears to be connected with the life of another Rama, who is distinguished as the Rama of the Dekhan. - Wheeler’s History of India Vol.II. Part IV.
27. The Ramayana contins an account of the exile which belongs to a much later period and cannot apparently have any connection with the earliest tradition. According to the later story Rama spent thirteen years of his exile in wandering with his wife and brother from one Brahmanical hermitage to another, in the country between the river Ganges and the river Godavari. These journeyings extended from the hill Chitra-Kuta in Bundelkhand, to the modern town of Nasik, near the sources of the Godavari, about seventy five miles to the north - west of the modern town of Bombay. The hermitages are sid to have been occupied by the old Rishies who composed the Vedic hymns, and who are represented as Brahmans although they must have flourished ages before the appearance of Brahmns. The whole narrative may therefore be dismissed as aprocryphal. - Ibid.
27. Brahman tales are generally untrustworthy for traditional history. The Ramayana is highly Brahamanical and its stories are fanciful and often absurd. - Ancient Indian Historical Traditions. - F.E. Pargiter.
28. Immediately following the epics about the first century A.D. the Puranas, mythological and speculative histories of universe began to be written. They were intended to promote several particular Brahmanical beliefs which had been developing since Vedic time. - Hindu View in Art. p. 35.
28. It is now generally admitted that a great deal of the ancient medieval myth and legend enshrined in Sanskrit epics and Puranas is of non-Aryan origin and even in Vedic mythology certin pre-Aryan elements are present. Puranic myths of the gods and legends of kings, heroes and sages in the form in which we find them in the Sanskrit works represent undoubted by a considerable amount of modification from their original forms whether Aryan or non-Aryan. The non-Aryan speaking masses of northern India became Aryanized in language and their tales and legends were retold as a matter of course in an Aryan language of their adoption. - S.K. Chatterji – Bulletin of the school of oriental studies, Vol.VIII (1935-1937).
28. In the earlier epoch prior to A.D. 1000 pre-Aryan legends were rendered from current Prakrit versions into Sanskrit and found a place in one or the other of the numerous Puranas, Upapuranas, Stalapuranas, and Mahatmyas and Tantras or even in Mahabharata and so were rised up to a level of pan Indian acceptance. - The history and culture of Indian People Vol.V., p.379.
28. In the 4th century A.D. Buddhism declined and there was a Brahmanical revival; and the Brahmans reedited some of the books on the religious and the civil laws and gave a new and popular shape to them. The old Puranas were also recasted about period and good many new ones written. - Collected works of R.G. Bhandarkar, Vol.II., p. 444.
28. The Puranas naturally lent themselves to augmentations and the Puranic Brahmans used their opportunities to the full, partly with further genuine traditions, but mostly with additions of Brahmanical stories and fables and doctrine and ritual matter.
Brahmanic tradition speaks from the Brahmanical stand point, describes events and expresses, feelings as they would appear to Brahmans, illustrates Brahmanical ideas, mintins and incalculates the dignity, sanctity, supremacy and even superhuman character of Brahmans, enunciates Brahmanical doctrines whatever subserved the interest of the Brahmans often enforcing the moral by means of marvellous incidents that not seldom are made up of absurd and utterly impossible detils. It often introduces kings becuse kings were their patrons, yet even so the Brahman’s dignity is never forgotten.
It is minly the Brahmanical mistakes and absurdities that have discredited Puranas. - Ancient Indian Historical Traditions pp. 37-39. - F.E. Pargeiter.
28. Agni Purana : A Purana (so named as supposed to have been communicated by Agni to Vasishtha) devoted to the glorification of Siva but of very various contents ritual, cosmical, ethical, military, legal, medical, rhetorical, grammatical, taken largely from earlier works. It is quite modern and has no legitimate clim to be regarded as a Purana. - The Century Cyclopedia of Names, Edited by Benjamin E. Smith.
28. Brahma Purana : One of the eighteen Puranas: so called as revealed by Brahma to Daksha. This Purana is placed first and therefore called adipurana. Its min object appears to be the promotion of the worship of Krishna. It describes the creation, the manvanthras of the life or period of Manu, the history of solar and lunar dynasties to the time of Krishna, Orissa with its temples and groves the life of Krishna, the mode of Yoga or contemplative devotion. It was not compiled earlier than the 13th or 14th century. - Ibid.
28. Brahmanda Purana : One of the eighteen Puranas so called as revealed by Brahma and contining an account of “the egg of Brahma” the mundane egg, and the future kalpas or days of Brahma. It is extent only in a number of un-authentic fragments. - Ibid.
28. Matsya Purana – A purana between fourteen and fifteen thousand stanzas complied from various materials; many chapters are identical with from Mahabharata. It is so called as narrated to Manu by Vishnu in the form of a fish. - Ibid.
28. Bagavata Purana – The Purana of Bhagavata or Vishnu, a book of great celebrity in India, exercising a more powerful influence upon the opinions of the people than any of the other Puranas. It consists 18,00 verses and is ascribed by Colebrooke to the grammarian Vopadeva, of about the 13th century A.D. Its most popular part the tenth book, which narrates the history of Krishna, has been translated into many vernaculars of India.-Ibid.
28. Skanda Purana – A Purana in which skanda is the narrator. It is sid to contin 81,800 stanzas and is an aggregation of many originally unrelated works and fragments. The most celebrated is the “Kashi Kandha” “Benares section” describing minutely the temples of Shiva at or near Benares, and giving direction for Shiva worship and greater part of Kasi Kandha antedates the first attack upon Benares by Mohmud Gazni – who reigned 997 – 1030 A.D. The Utkala khanda is the section explining the holiness of Orissa the inhabitants of which were known as Utkalas. - Ibid.
28. Linga Purana – The Purana in which Shiva explins the object of life : virtue, wealth, pleasure and final liberation. It contins 11,000 stanzas and is not earlier than the 8th or 9th century.
28. Vamana Purana – A Purana extended to about 7000 stanzas, and contining among other things, an account of the dwarf incarnation of Vishnu. It is of very recent origin having been compiled apparently only three or four centuries ago. - Ibid.
30. The social distinctions of Vedic times were those of occupation and of colour (Varna) which imposed race marked by difference of dress – white for Brahmans, red for Kshatrias, yellow for Vaisias and black for Sudras. The Aryan ethnical type which had closely intermingled with the non-Aryan population before the caste system was fully developed never continued more than a small fraction even of the population of the north. - A Short History of Indian – p. 29 – Havell.
29. Dharmashastra – The whole body of Hindu law; more specially the laws ascribed to Manu; Yajnavalkya and other inspired sages. These works are generally in three parts : (1) Achara, rules of conduct (2) Vyavahara, judicature, prayashchitta, penance. The inspired law givers are spoken as eighteen but forty two are mentioned. Manu and Yajnavalkya stand at their head. – Century Cyclopedia of names.
31. Brahman priests, Buddhists and Jaina ascetics must have reached the land before the Christian era, and established themselves at the courts of ruling princes where they found schools of learning and exercised their influence on the thought of the times. The local gods, national deified heroes, and sacrificial cults of the people became in time absorbed into Brahmanism – A Literary History of India p. 310 – R.W. Frazer.
33. When the Brahmans settled in Southern India and the ancient Tamil Rajahs desiring to secure the benefit of the Yagas, accepted to the fire priests a supreme position to the society, the Brahmans naturally tried to introduce Socio – religious organization in Tamil religion – pre-aryan Tamil Culture p.20 – P.T.S. Iyengar.
32. Even in the first century B.C. very little Aryan influence had penetrated to the extreme south. Some Brahman colonists settled in the Dravidian countries and intermarried with the priest caste of the natives, but on the whole they made very little impression on the race. South Indian tradition records numerous instances of the Brahman as taking wives from the lower castes. In many cases non-Brahmans were admitted into the Brahmana caste as sufficient Brahmans were not avilable when the reformed Indo Aryan religion obtined preference. The non-aryan magicians and the Dravidian priests became Brahmans – Prehistoric Ancient and Hindu India pp. 30, 37, 120 – R.D. Banerje.
32. There have been three classes of Brahmans throughtout Indian history namely (1) the ascetic devote and teacher, the Rishi or Muni (2) The priest and spiritual guide of kings, nobles and people (3) The minister of state royal officer and those who followed secular employments – Ancient Indian Historical Traditions – p. 62 – F.E. Pargiter.
32. Though in the long years that preceded the first century A.D. a few Aryans had penetrated the natural barrier of the Vindhyas and traversed the region beyond, there was not a definite attempt in founding fresh empires or settlements in the Dekhan till the date. The Pallavas were almost the first people to acquire dominians in the south. Their success in the direction seems to have attracted their followers in the north. The Rashtrakutas and the Gangas were not slow to take similar advantages – Pallavas had their own alphabet which is now known to us as the Pallava-Grantha – Dr. Burnel calls it the Eastern Chera characters and states that it should have first come to be employed in Thondimandalam in the 4th century A.D. – Historical sketches of ancient Dekhan. p.20 – K.V. Subramanya Iyer (Madras 1917).
34. Brahmanism also flourished and most of the Satavahana rulers were devoted to it. The third king of the line performed a number of Vedic sacrifices and even named one of his sons Vedisri – A history of South India p. 95. – K.A. Nilakanta Sastri.
35. The Pallavas were followers of the Brahmanical religion and made gifts of land to gods and Brahmans in the belief that they would thereby secure health, prosperity and victory in war. Excemption of tax-action was allowed on all gifts of land to Brahmins who were held, in theory at any rate, to be entitled to a total of eighteen such immunities. This is a continuation and development of Satavahana practice, for the pallava kings also followed the Brahmanical religion, worshipped Siva and Vishnu and performed sacrifies - Ibid.
36. Religious condition that followed in the Kadamba and Ganga kingdoms were very much the same as those in contemporary Pallava kingdom – Ibid p. 105.
36. The Kadambas were a Brahman family which derived its descent from Hariti and belonged to the Manavya gotra. They were devoted to the study of the Vedas and the performance of vedic sacrifices. The Kadamba king Mayurasarman entered ghatika (college) at Kanchipuram with the intention of studying the entire Veda – Ibdi p. 105.
36. In Egypt the names of the gods were never uttered. It was a crime among the Jews to utter the name of Jawah – The mothers Vol. III p. 109.
The great name of god Jhwh was commonly called tetra gamma which was never pronounced and only written was associated with the twelve tribes of Isrel – Amulets and superstition, p. 379. – Sir. E.A. Wallis & Budge K.T.

Katyayana, the grammarian, Baudhayana the smirthi writer, and possibly Apastamba also were south Indians, but we do not know to which part of south India they exactly belonged – Malayalam and other Languages p. 1249 – Proceedings and Transactions of the 9th All India Oriental Conference, Trivandram Dec. 1937.
38. It was for many years universally believed the Sanskrit was the mother tongue of which all languages could be traced. The theory was not by far as absurd as that which had been set up some time previously by religious zealots who from an exaggerated regard untutored by science for all that is connected with the inspired books of our creed went so far as to assert that Hebrew was the mother of all the languages in the world – Vedic India p. 58 – Regozen.
39. Less than a thousand years ago the Agamas were looked on as unuthoritative and Yamuna, in founding the modern Vaishnava Visishtadvita School felt it necessary to write the Agamapramanya the authoritativeness of the Agamas. Today, however freely scraps of Upanishads are quoted in discussions, the actual opinions and religious practices of the Hindus are taken entirely from the Agamas. For this and other reasons the Agamas have been kept secret – Outlines of Indian Philosophy p. IV. – P.T.S. Iyengar.
39. The worship of Siva or Vishnu or Sakti in temples or houses was considered a heresy by the Vedantis till in the tenth century Yamunacharya wrote the Agama Pramanya and Ramanucharya in the next century blended the Vaishnava rites and concepts and Vedic practices tents on the whole – Stone age in Inda p. 52. – P.T.S. Iyengar.
40. Saivat radition as preserved in Periyapuranam has memories of mutts organized by Appar and other non-Brahman Saiva sints. These were their spiritual homes. When the temple cult came to be codified and conventionalized with the help of *Gauda Brahmins and other north Indian Saivites during the Chola revival the mutt became the necessary adjunct of the temple presided over by Brahman for regulating and supervising the rituals. Slowly the objection to non- Brahmans renouncing the world and becoming the heads of mutts came to be established. The non-Brahman ascetics had to resort to caves and their mutts came to be known as “Kugi”. When the number and power of these non-Brahman mutts increased the orthodox people inspired a group of their followers to raze to ground these non-Brahman mutts and this is mentioned as Kugi idi kalagam in inscriptions of the reign of Kulotunga III. A theory was enunciated that the philosophic truths should be learnt from the Vedas direct and not through vernacular works. The Vaishnavite philosophers specially of the Tenkali persuation exposed the hollowness of these pretensions. The Guru Namachivayar of the 16th century (S.I.I.Vol.I No.58) shows that this distinction of Kugi and mutt was still prevalent as late as the 16th century. In this century a dispute arose whether the non-Brahmans were entitled to become Sanyasins and Chinna Chevvappa Nayak, the chieftin of the Vijayanagar emperors Krishnadevaraya and Accuta Raya referred this to Sivagra Yogi, a Brahman ascetic. He gave his decision in favour of the non-Brahmans in the form of an elaborate thesis “Saiva Sannyasa Paddhati” Krishnadevaraya a Vaishnavite, could not have tolerated the arrogance of caste in the spiritual sphere. We find therefore the great non-Brahman mutts growing and developing in the 16th century – The notes on the Tamil Plutarch. – Prof. T.P. Meenakshisundaram.
41. No.471 of 1912 records the gift of such a monastary for a Saiva sint by a village, which also provided for the feeding of all strangers who might visit it. The property of this monastry was confiscated in the twenty second year of Kulotunga Chola III when there was a general crusade aginst the non-Brahmanical Saiva mathas instigated by the Brahmans – Local Government in Ancient India p. 279 – R.K. Mookerji.
42. Sanskrit learning tended to be monopoly of Brahmins, though there were exceptions, and it was particularly encouraged by means of large special endowments – A History of South India, p. 312.
44. The scheme of four varunas could not well spread among the Tamils. It only led to the confusion of caste and prevalence of social jealousies and have characterized the life of South India for a thousand five hundred years; for we learn from Thevaram of Thirunavukkarasu Nayanar that there was in his day, as there is to-day, a consciousness of rivarlry, between Brahman and non-Brahmans as they were then called Aryan and Tamilian – Pre-aryan Tamil Culture. P. 20 – P.T.S. Iyengar.
43. But when the subject matter and the contents of the Agamas and the Vedas are closely examined and studied it will be found that the Agamas and the Vedas stand altogether apart as poles as under. – The Philosophy of the Lingayats – S.K. Sakhare.
45. We might see that it would be more correct to describe Indian religion as Dravidian religion stimulated and modified by the ideas of Aryan invaders. For the great deities in Hinduism Siva, Krishna, Rama, Durga and some of its most essential doctrines such as metempsychosis and divine incarnations are either totally unknown to the Veda or obscurely adumbrated in it. The chief characterstics of mature Indian religion are characterstics of an area not of a race, and they are not the characterstics of religion of Persia, Greece or other Aryan lands. – Hinduism and Buddhism, p. XV. Sir. Charles Elliot.

The influence of the Dravidians on the Culture of India has been ignored, becuse the literature which records the development of the Hindu religion in India was the work of a hostile priesthood, whose only object was to magnify its own pretentions and decry everything Dravidian – Dravidian India, p. 119.– T.R. Sesha Iyengar.
46. At any rate we may be on our guard aginst looking at everything through Aryan or Brahmanical spectacles … that almost everything has passed into written form has been cast in an Aryan mould. For real history Brahmanic writers never cared anything; early events and family origins invariably assume a mythic guise; everything about non-Aryan race is either omitted or only noticed the conquest of the ‘twice’ over the ‘demons’ and ‘barberians’ – The Indian Village Community, p. 91 – B.H.Barden Powell. M.A., C.I.E.
46. A variety of cuses partly political and partly literary, has tended to the belittlement of peninsular India’s contribution of the history both of India and of the whole world in large. The time is ripe for South India to champion her own cuse and assert her clims to recognition – F.R.Richards I.C.S., M.A., M.R.A.S., F.R.A.S. – The quarterly Journal of the Mythic Socity Vol. IV.
The early tribes of Bengal Dravidian speakers minly were well organized, and seem to have possessed a culture of their own. The early history of Burma and Siam tells us that at a time when the Tibeto – Chinese tribes, Burmese and Tai had not yet arrived on the scene, and these centres were inhabited by only Monkhmer peoples, Dravidians from Bengal and Kalinga were emigrating into these lands, and becoming the ruling race there. Later when these non-Aryans from India assimilated Brahmanic culture, their princes climed connection with the ancient royal house of Aryan upper India (a thing which was repeated in the case of the new Rajput clans at a later period) and introduced among the Mons and Khmers in times post Christ the Sanskrit language as well as traditions connected with Hastinapura and Ayodya – The Development of Bengali Language p.41 – S.K. Chatterji.
The modern dialects of Northern India now called Sanskritic or Gaudian, have a fundamental grammatical frame work and a scheme of syntax, the same as that of the Dravidian dialects, so much so that sentences from the one set of dialects can be translated into one of the other set of dialects by the substitution of word for word, without cusing any breach of idium. – History of the Tamils, p.2 – P.T.S. Iyengar (1929).
Dravidian stratum in Sanskrit has been discussed by several scholars and Kittel in Kannada dictionary has shown 450 Sanskrit words with possible Dravidian connections. A few other words in both Sanskrit and Prakrit and vernaculars have subsequently been suggested as being of Dravidian origin by other scholars – The Journal of the Greater India Society Vol. III (1936) Prof. Sunitii Kumar Chatterji.

civaṉ
muṉṉuri
ivvulakiṉ āṅkāṅku vaḻaṅkum periya veḷḷap perukkip paṟṟiya paḻiya varalāṟukaḷik koṇṭu makkaṭ kulam, ātiyil oru naṭu iṭattiṟ perukiyiruntu piṉpu ulakiṉ pala iṭaṅkaḷukkup pirintu ceṉṟu paṟpala kulaṅkaḷ pōṟ perukiṟṟu eṉap paḻañ carittirak kārarum, moḻi ārāycciyāḷarum karutukiṉṟaṉar. ulaka makkaḷiṉ camayattip paṟṟi naṉku ārāynta vesrap (Westropp) eṉṉum āciriyar muṟkāla makkaḷiṉ camayam taṉittaṉiyē tōṉṟi vaḷarcci yaṭintataṉṟu; ellāc camayaṅkaḷukkum aṭippaṭi oṉṟē eṉak kūṟiyuḷḷār. ulakil tōṉṟiyirunta paḻiya nākarikaṅkaḷukkellām mikap paḻimi uṭiyatu cintu veḷi nākarikameṉap paḻimi ārāycciyil taliciṟanta amerikkap pērāciriyarkaḷākiya pirāṅ pōrṭ (Professor Frankfort), vil tuṟaṇṭ (Wil Durant) mutaliyōr kūṟi yuḷḷaṉar. ulaka nākarikattukku aṭippaṭi yiluḷḷatu intiya nākarika meṉpatum, intiya nākarikameṉpatu tirāviṭa nākarikameṉpatum mēṟpula ārāycci aṟiñarkaḷāl naṉku ārāyntu kāṭṭappaṭ ṭuḷḷaṉa. ulaka moḻikaḷ, ulaka nākarikaṅkaḷukkuḷ toṭarpu kāṇappaṭuvatu pōlavē, tamiḻaruṭiya civa vaṇakkattukkum ulaka camayaṅkaḷukkum oṟṟumi kāṇappaṭukiṉṟatu. paḻiya tamiḻ makkaḷiṉ civa vaṇakkattiṉ uṟaḻcci piṟaḻccikaḷē iṉṟiya ulaka mataṅkaḷākum eṉpatik kāṭṭuvatu kaṭiṉamāka irukkavilli. avvāṟiruntum ittuṟiyil tamiḻ aṟiñar ūṉṟi ārāycci ceytu, ak karutti ulakukku veḷiyiṭātiruppatu peruṅkuṟiyākum. civamatamē ulaka matam eṉpati, nām, paṟpala mēṟpula ārāycci aṟiñar kaṇṭa muṭivukaḷi ēṟṟa ēṟṟa iṭaṅkaḷil mēṟkōḷkaḷāka eṭuttuk kāṭṭiyum, āṅkāṅku ulakiṉ pala pākaṅkaḷil kāṇappaṭukiṉṟa, iṉṟum namatu nāṭṭil vaḻipaṭap paṭuvaṉapōṉṟa tāykkaṭavuḷ, tantik kaṭavuḷarkaḷiṉ vaṭivaṅkaḷi paṭaṅkaḷamittuk kāṭṭiyum teḷḷitiṉ viḷakkiyuḷḷōm. “civa camayamē camayam camayā tītap paḻamporuḷ” eṉṉun tāyumāṉa aṭikaḷiṉ kūṟṟu iṉṟiya ārāycciyil uṇmiyākavē tikaḻkiṉṟatu.
ceṉṉi
15.2.1947 na.ci.kantiyā.
civaṉ
tōṟṟuvāy
mika muṟkālattil ivvulaka makkaḷ ellōrukkum potuvāṉa koḷkikaḷ pala iruntaṉa. avikaḷuḷ camayamum oṉṟu. ellā makkaḷum orēvakiyākak kikkoṇṭa camayamē nāḷaṭivil ciṟitu ciṟitāka vēṟupaṭṭu iṉṟiya pala camayaṅkaḷākak kāṇappaṭukiṉṟatu. ellā camayaṅkaḷiṉ paḻimiyi nōkki ārāyntu celliṉ avi ellām oru taṉi matattiṟ ceṉṟu muṭivaṭitalik kāṇalām.
